blocks.text: Here are the biggest headlines from India on Tuesday, November 24:
November 24, 2026
India deepens authoritarian slide under Modi — Report

blocks.caption: Modi has spent over 12 years as India's premierImage: Seshadri Sukumar/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Prime Minister Modi's Hindu nationalist government has "systematically weakened" institutions meant to protect human rights and democratic freedoms, a scathing new report by Human Rights Watch concluded.

In a 95-page report titled 'So What's This Democracy We're Talking About?: Modi's Authoritarian Playbook in India,' the watchdog found that the right-wing Bharatiya Janata Party-led (BJP) government is undermining parliamentary procedures, suppressing opposition and weaponzing investigative agencies for political ends.
It also found that the government has weakened constitutional and statutory bodies meant to protect democratic freedoms and the rights of the people.
India's 'Cockroach' protesters claim online censorship
'Authoritarian playbook'

"Over the past decade, the Modi government has been hollowing out India’s independent institutions that are critical to checking executive power and protecting civil liberties," said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch.

"The government has eroded the rule of law and promoted Hindu majoritarianism, rolling back human rights protections, undermining the rights of marginalized communities, and deepening India's authoritarian slide."

The report further claimed the Election Commission of India and the Supreme Court — both independent bodies — failed to uphold fundamental freedoms, pointing to the elimination of millions of voter names from India's electoral rolls in a controversial exercise.

blocks.caption: Nationwide protests against deleted voter names broke out in India in October, only to be met with widespread detentionsImage: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

blocks.text: "The Modi administration's actions over the past decade are not isolated institutional failures but mutually reinforcing elements of an authoritarian playbook," Human Rights Watch said.
"India's allies should press the Modi government to end its assault on independent institutions and restore checks on executive power," Pearson said.
The BJP or Modi's government is yet to comment on the report which was published Tuesday morning. However, both have dismissed similar criticisms in the past.

articles.title: South Korea tells island residents to take shelter after Russian military aircraft approach
articles.summary:
The order was issued after aircraft entered the country’s air defence identification zone over the island of Ulleungdo

Residents of a remote South Korean island were ordered to take shelter…

blocks.text: Residents of a remote South Korean island were ordered to take shelter on Tuesday morning after several Russian military aircraft came close to entering its airspace, prompting a pre-emptive alert from the military that anticipated a violation.
The defence ministry said it would summon the Russian defence attaché on Tuesday afternoon to lodge a strong protest.

The joint chiefs of staff (JCS) said the aircraft had entered the country’s air defence identification zone over the Sea of Japan – known in South Korea as the East Sea – and approached the island of Ulleungdo. It did not specify how many Russian aircraft were involved, but South Korean air force jets were scrambled before the aircraft left.

A JCS spokesperson, Jang Do-young, said the aircraft had approached “to the point just before violating Ulleungdo’s airspace” and that, because military aircraft move very fast, a violation was anticipated.
The alert was issued pre-emptively to protect residents, he said.

The interior ministry issued the emergency alert at 7.52am to residents of Ulleungdo, a volcanic island of about 8,700 people 120km off the east coast, telling them to take shelter. The English portion of the message read: “EVACUATION, AIR RAID”.

Television broadcasts were interrupted by on-screen warnings telling residents to “prepare to evacuate to a nearby underground shelter facility and listen to broadcasting”. The alert was lifted at 7.55am.

On the island, sirens sounded and residents reportedly heard the noise of fighter jets. Jeong Hae-seung, 41, who was working on a building site, told the Hankyoreh newspaper he ran out of his workplace the moment the text arrived.

blocks.caption: A man jogs past a lighthouse at Jeodong port on the island of Ulleungdo. Photograph: Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “I went outside wondering what on earth was going on, and the civil defence broadcast was playing, but I couldn’t make out what it was saying,” he said.
Baek Un-bae, who lives on the island, told broadcaster YTN that an elderly resident had telephoned him asking whether war had broken out.
“Older people have no access to the media, so all they hear is the warning broadcast and they are too alarmed to know what to do,” he said.
Others said they did not hear the sirens at all, with windows shut against the cold and strong winds blowing.
A second message, sent by North Gyeongsang province, which administers Ulleungdo, said a flying object “presumed to be a North Korean aircraft” had left the danger zone.
The province said it had mistakenly taken the wording from its routine drill messages, changed only the time and sent it in error.
Jang described the alert as unusual but said he could not confirm whether it was the first of its kind.
Tuesday’s incident was the fourth known entry by Russian military aircraft into the zone this year and the second in a week.

An air defence identification zone is not sovereign airspace, but countries establish such zones beyond their own airspace to identify incoming military flights early. While submitting a flight plan in advance is international practice, entering an identification zone without prior notification does not in itself violate international law.
Russia argues that the Korean zone has no basis in international law and does not recognise Seoul’s authority over it, and has repeatedly flown into it without notice.
According to data submitted to parliament, about 60 Russian entries without prior notification were recorded in the five years to 2024, compared with about 430 by Chinese aircraft.

Seoul previously summoned Russia’s defence attaché in March 2025 after eight entries in 10 days. At the time, it was the first such summons since a Russian aircraft violated South Korean airspace in 2019 and South Korean jets fired warning shots.

articles.title: Social media companies could be fined 5% of global revenue after Labor and Greens join forces on online safety laws
articles.summary: Individual Australians will be able to sue big tech firms for harm suffered online under compromise deal

blocks.text: Big tech companies may face “multibillion-dollar” fines and individuals could sue social media companies in court under Australia’s new digital duty of care laws, with the Greens to support the bill’s passage after extracting major amendments from Labor.
From late 2027, Australians will also be able opt out of addictive online algorithms under the new legislation, while the “endless scroll” of social media feeds may also cease.

The communications minister, Anika Wells, confirmed that, in extreme breaches, social media and tech companies could face fines of up to 5% of their global revenue if they flout the new laws. She said she had already met with the US ambassador, David Brat, to discuss the laws, and had stared down potential legal challenges from some of the world’s most powerful firms.
“I was at the high court a couple of weeks ago as the second respondent in the case against the social media minimum age. If people want to have another go, bring it on,” Wells said on Tuesday.

The government’s legislation will pass parliament this week, potentially as soon as Tuesday afternoon, after the Greens agreed to support the bill after intense negotiations. The Coalition had opposed the laws from the outset, citing free speech and censorship concerns, leaving the Greens to negotiate with Labor.

The planned framework would apply new online safety standards to social media, games, apps and chatbots. Labor said it would place “an overarching obligation” on tech platforms “to provide a safe online environment for all Australians” and replace a range of existing online codes and standards with a broader duty-of-care requirement to protect users from certain “harmful” content. Wells had suggested content promoting misogyny, terrorism, suicide, self-harm and eating disorders would be captured by the laws.

Following discussions with the Greens, Wells on Tuesday confirmed amendments to the bill would see Australians given a “private right of action” – a local equivalent to successful laws in the US allowing citizens to sue large companies.
The government will consider setting up an independent ombudsman or watchdog for big tech, and the maximum fines for breaches of rules could reach $109m, or up to 5% of global revenue.
The moves could draw the ire of US-based tech giants and the Trump administration.

Wells has previously said Donald Trump’s Truth Social platform would be subject to the laws, and said the government had committed to “constructive dialogue” with the US, including during her Tuesday meeting with Brat.
“I think we would say there are points of differences, and we’re ironing them out,” she said.
Meta, Google, TikTok and Snapchat were contacted for comment.

Other major changes to the bill include adding “addictive” features to the list of risks that tech platforms must address, and clarifying the definitions of “hostile attitudes to women and gender equality”. Wells said this was “not about disagreeing with feminism or expressing an opinion”, but would force tech platforms to avoid exposing children to content promoting hatred of women, including violence, death threats, coercion or harassment.
after newsletter promotion
She has previously stated “manosphere podcasts” would not be affected.
Amendments to the bill will also expand eSafety Commissioner powers to remove “nudify” apps and content, and stronger privacy protections.
“The Greens have long campaigned for big tech to be held accountable for the harm they profit off online,” the Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young said on Tuesday.

The party had long pressed for stronger fines, an ombudsman scheme and stronger action on addictive design features. Hanson-Young said that provision would have the effect of “dumping the doomscroll with rules that force tech companies to prevent harm from their addictive design feature”.
This would go alongside original requirements for social media platforms to offer an “opt-out” feature for its algorithm and suggested content.

Wells said those elements would come into force 12 months after the laws passed. She nominated design features such as “the toxic popularity meters, the endless scroll” as those which could be banned under the addictive features stipulation, but said final decisions would be made by eSafety.
The Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman, which has volunteered to act as a big tech watchdog, welcomed the move to set up an independent complaints mechanism.
“Online services are a core part of our lives. It’s great that Australians will soon have access to a free, fair and independent dispute resolution scheme when big tech gets things wrong.”

articles.title: [Vantage Point] Boardroom gymnastics, retail stakes: Unpacking the Rockwell deal
articles.summary: FPH owes investors proof that nearly P16 billion in cash beats keeping a profitable property arm, just as Rockwell’s minorities deserve full clarity before deciding whether to stay put or cash out

blocks.text: Too often, financial reporting treats corporate dealmaking like a spectator sport for billionaires — fixating on which tycoon is buying control, which conglomerate is cashing out, and how much changes hands at the top.
Lost in the noise is what these corporate intramurals mean for the thousands of ordinary public investors whose capital sustains market valuations.
First Philippine Holdings’ (FPH) proposed sale of its controlling stake in Rockwell Land to Crème Investment Corporation for nearly P16 billion is a textbook case.

Strip away the prominent surnames, and two practical questions remain for everyday shareholders on both sides: Are FPH investors getting fair value for surrendering a profitable business, and will Rockwell’s minorities get enough hard facts to make an informed choice?

Signed on November 13, the deal carries an amended 11-month closing deadline measured from signing, down from 12 months, and awaits Philippine Competition Commission approval plus a mandatory tender offer for Rockwell’s remaining public shares. A signed agreement is only the opening act, not a finished sale.

For small investors reading the fine print, the headline numbers require unpacking. The P15.916-billion price tag covers P15.888 billion for 5.296 billion common shares at P3 apiece, plus P27.5 million for 2.75 billion preferred shares at P0.01 each.

While headlines highlight a 90.74% combined stake, measuring FPH’s common shares against Rockwell’s 6.117 billion outstanding common shares puts its common equity holding at roughly 86.58%. The combined percentage includes preferred stock; it is not the common-share stake being sold.

Equally crucial is where the money goes. Upon closing, the P15.916 billion gross consideration goes to FPH, not Rockwell. Because this is a secondary sale of existing stock rather than a capital raise, Rockwell receives zero fresh cash to build towers, pay down debt, or fund dividends. Minorities weighing whether to stay invested must recognize that the sale itself adds no cash to Rockwell’s balance sheet.
On the FPH side, small shareholders must temper expectations. Dividing P15.916 billion by FPH’s 424.5 million outstanding common shares equates to roughly P37.49 per share.
That merely measures deal scale — not a guaranteed special dividend or an automatic share-price jump. Taxes, transaction fees, and carrying value will ultimately dictate what hits the bottom line.

FPH did take visible steps to validate the P3 sale price. Adviser BDO Capital & Investment Corporation valued Rockwell’s common shares between P2.47 and P3.09 — putting the price near the top of the range — while independent directors, external counsel, and buyer adviser AlphaPrimus Advisors were brought in.

Yet governance checklists cannot replace transparent math. Public investors deserve to see how that valuation treated project spending, borrowing costs, cash collections, and recurring commercial income — and whether it included a control premium rather than pricing the block like an illiquid minority stake.

Rockwell’s latest results make this scrutiny even more urgent. FPH is not unloading a troubled unit: nine-month revenue climbed to P19.317 billion from P14.996 billion a year earlier, lifting profit attributable to parent shareholders by roughly 21.5% to P3.788 billion from P3.117 billion.

Though third-quarter attributable profit dipped about 10.7% to P1.076 billion from P1.205 billion — as nine-month non-operating expenses rose to P2.389 billion from P1.359 billion — one softer quarter hardly invalidates Rockwell’s long-term case.

At P3 per share, the deal values Rockwell at roughly 3.4 times trailing 12-month earnings of P0.88 per share. On paper, 3.4 times looks like a bargain for the buyer. While property accounting profits depend heavily on construction progress, revenue recognition, and financing costs — meaning net income rarely equals free cash — management must explain why such a modest multiple is fair to sellers.

Broker commentary underscores this tug-of-war between instant cash and lost income. Online trading platform COL Financial noted that the P15.9-billion consideration represents a 99% premium over its estimated net asset value for FPH’s Rockwell stake, raising its fair-value estimate for FPH by 11.8%. Yet COL also estimated that Rockwell accounts for roughly 25% of FPH’s net income. Unlocking asset value today leaves a sizable earnings hole tomorrow.

FPH says the proceeds will fund energy, infrastructure, and other growth ventures. Rotating capital out of mature assets makes sense, provided retail investors are told the recurring profits sacrificed, net cash left after costs, and expected returns from replacement projects — with any disposal gain reported separately from core earnings.

Meanwhile, Rockwell’s small shareholders face a pivotal choice once formal tender documents arrive. Beyond payment timelines and funding certainty, they must scrutinize the buyer’s plans. The tender price and complete terms still require confirmation. A change in control does not automatically trigger delisting, but tender acceptances could reduce public ownership below the PSE’s 10% minimum. Rockwell’s reported free float was 13.05% before the announcement. Anyone staying invested must weigh potential shifts in governance, debt appetite, and trading liquidity.

Finally, FPH’s disclosure that certain directors of the seller and buyer are related within the fourth civil degree raises the bar for accountability. Family ties do not prove wrongdoing, but detailing independent board vetting and director abstentions is essential if small investors are to trust the process.

Rockwell’s change-in-control filing left the buyer’s material relationships and directors’ transaction interests marked “to follow.” Those disclosures need completion before minorities decide whether to tender.

Public markets thrive only when everyday shareholders are treated as true stakeholders rather than passive bystanders to boardroom deals. FPH owes investors proof that nearly P16 billion in cash beats keeping a profitable property arm, just as Rockwell’s minorities deserve full clarity before deciding whether to stay put or cash out.

This analysis draws from FPH’s November 16 amended transaction disclosure, Rockwell’s ownership disclosure, its September 2026 quarterly financial report, and COL Financial’s November 13 research note. Ownership percentages, per-share proceeds, earnings growth, and the earnings multiple are our calculations; COL’s valuation and contribution estimates remain explicitly attributed.
I welcome your views on these and other issues where decisions made in power shape the country’s economic future. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Ombudsman prosecutor: No document shows Romualdez directed Co on budget matters
articles.summary: A prosecution witness said Tuesday there were no documents showing former House speaker and Leyte Representative Martin Romualdez directed former House appropriations panel chairperson Zaldy Co of…

blocks.text: 'CENTRAL FIGURES ARE NEVER THE FRONT'
Published November 24, 2026 11:49am

A prosecution witness said Tuesday there were no documents showing former House speaker and Leyte Representative Martin Romualdez directed former House appropriations panel chairperson Zaldy Co of Ako Bicol party-list on budget matters.

Assistant Special Prosecutor Joshua Tan of the Office of the Ombudsman made the testimony during the bail hearing of Romualdez, who is facing a P7.4-billion plunder case alongside Co and others over their alleged links to the flood control kickback scheme.

During the cross examination of Romualdez's counsel Rashel Pomoy, Tan was asked if there were documents showing that Romualdez provided instructions to Co on budget allocations. It has been the prosecution's theory that Romualdez was the central figure in the budget for flood control projects, and that it was Co who identified projects and made insertions in the proposed budget.
Tan replied, "None."

Asked by Pomoy if the prosecution's argument of Romualdez giving instructions to Co was based on inference, Tan replied, "Yes," but qualified it by saying it was "based on the evidence gathered by the Special Panel of Investigators."

Pomoy also asked Tan if Ombudsman investigators found documents from a contractor, Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) personnel, or any other contract showing that Romualdez received commission from any of them, Tan replied: "None."
Tan also confirmed that state witness Roberto Bernardo, a former Public Works undersecretary, only testified that he only dealt with Co, not Romualdez.
Central figures
During the redirect examination by Deputy Special Prosecutor Omar Sagadal, Tan said, "central figures are never the front."
“You [as a central figure] will never be at the front yourself. Otherwise, it would be pointless,” Tan said.
Tan said there were also three sets of independent evidence showing that pieces of luggage containing money were delivered to property registered under Romualdez.
"If that [delivery] is true, what would be the reason for that," Tan said.

According to Tan, the Ombudsman was still investigating Romualdez and apparent associate Jose Paras for a separate money laundering offense due to the latter's purchase of two properties in Forbes Park, which the prosecution argues are way above the financial capacity of Paras.
The prosecution alleges that the companies used by Paras to buy the properties are linked to Romualdez, making the former House speaker the real buyer.
Tan, however, said Romualdez is not a stockholder in the Golden Pheasant and Brightnews firms used by Paras to make such purchases. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Manila court orders arrest of Atong Ang, ex-cop in missing sabungeros case
articles.summary: A Manila court has issued a warrant of arrest against fugitive tycoon Atong Ang and former police officer Ryan Jay Orapa.

blocks.text: November 24, 2026 | 10:48am

Businessman Charlie "Atong" Ang, accompanied by his lawyer Lorna Kapunan, files criminal charges before the Mandaluyong City Prosecutor's Office on July 3, 2025 against Julie "Dondon" Patidongan and Alan Bantiles for accusations related to the case of "missing sabungeros."
The STAR / Michael Varcas
MANILA, Philippines — A Manila court has issued a warrant of arrest against fugitive tycoon Atong Ang and former police officer Ryan Jay Orapa.

In a message to reporters on Tuesday, November 24, Department of Justice spokesperson Polo Martinez said that the Manila Regional Trial Court Branch 175 issued the arrest warrant against Ang and Orapa on October 30.
“In its Order, the court found sufficient evidence to establish probable cause to hold both accused for trial for the offenses charged,” Martinez said.
The charges against Ang and Orapa are kidnapping and serious illegal detention. The said charges are non-bailable.
This came after the Manila court granted the prosecution’s motion to amend the information in the Manila Arena case, after the prosecution panel found prima facie evidence to charge Ang and Orapa.
However, one of the accused successfully sought the inhibition of Branch 185’s presiding judge, prompting the re-raffling of the case to Branch 175, according to Martinez.

Ang’s camp also moved to defer arraignment and suspend proceedings pending its petition for review with the DOJ, with the court noting the motion while the parties await further action and the next hearing date.
Ang has been in hiding since January 2026, after courts in Laguna and Batangas issued arrest warrants against him in connection with the missing-sabungeros cases. He has not been arrested since then.
Ang denies all the allegations against him.

articles.title: China sentences official to death for spying for foreign country
articles.summary:
Accused official leaked national secrets to unnamed country and received payments worth over $150,000, state-linked publisher says

A Chinese official has been sentenced to death for spying…

blocks.text: A Chinese official has been sentenced to death for spying for a foreign country, a government-linked publisher has said.

Gold Wall Press, a publishing company associated with China’s national administration of state secrets protection, said the convicted person was surnamed Ma and was approached and recruited by an unnamed foreign intelligence service while working abroad.

Chinese courts typically do not publish information about state security cases, but in recent years the powerful ministry of state security and Gold Wall Press have increasingly publicised arrests, as well as using social media, movies and comics to promote warnings about espionage.

The statement on Monday said Ma had signed a cooperation agreement containing clauses on “confidentiality” and “loyalty” and received fixed monthly payments. In total, it said, he provided 35 pieces of information that were classified as national secrets and received payments worth more than 1m yuan ($150,000).

An intelligence operative identified as Kailin “frequently arranged to meet with Ma, hoping to engage with him more”, citing an interest in learning Chinese, the statement said. Kailin later introduced him to a colleague who threatened to report his earlier disclosures to Chinese authorities if he refused to cooperate.

After returning to China, Ma continued to gather intelligence for the foreign agency, which provided him with a laptop, the statement said. He used his position to collect material from classified documents during the day and transmitted it overseas at night via an espionage website.
The statement did not identify the countries involved, or say when or where he was sentenced or whether he had already been executed.
The case comes as US intelligence has been publicising its own efforts to recruit sources in China. The five most-viewed videos on the CIA’s YouTube channel are recruiting advertisements in Mandarin.

“This shocking case serves as yet another wake-up call,” the Gold Wall Press said, warning that foreign intelligence agencies were “cunning” and used emotional ties, financial interests and threats to recruit people in key positions.
The statement also urged officials to remain vigilant, strengthen their loyalty to the Communist party, protect state secrets and guard against foreign recruitment.

In 2023 Beijing broadened its anti-espionage law, expanding the definition of espionage and strengthening the investigative powers of state security authorities. The following year it revised its state secrets law to extend restrictions on sensitive information to so-called “work secrets”.
Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li

articles.title: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports
articles.summary: German media said Russia planned to launch a satellite with a nuclear warhead into space in coming weeks.

blocks.text: Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after reports that Russia was preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.

Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media outlets. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.
Asked about the reports, Rutte said: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element."
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hadn't seen the latest reports but dismissed reports citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".
The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".
Rutte told the press conference in Berlin that Nato had a variety of response options.
"When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary," he said.

Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, the reports by broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites.

Standing alongside Rutte, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue".
"Reports that Russia is planning to introduce nuclear weaponry into space are not new, yet they remain no less shocking," he said.

A German government spokesman earlier also did not confirm or deny the reports, but said it was taking the reports "very seriously", AFP reported. The spokesman, however, warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".
Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, said having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario", German paper Handelsblatt reported.

Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit. Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.
In 2024 the US claimed Russia was developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation.
"Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time.

In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".

articles.title: The Sky Cable paradox: From ABS-CBN’s second business to its burden
articles.summary: Can Sky Cable become financially strong enough to stop depending on the company it was supposed to help?

blocks.text: ABS-CBN spent decades building Sky Cable into a second business that could make money outside of free television. It bought smaller cable companies, expanded into home internet and satellite TV, and borrowed billions of pesos to pay for that growth. Those choices made sense at the time, but some of the technologies Sky bet on eventually fell behind newer rivals and changing viewer habits. The bank loans, however, never went away. What started as a plan to make ABS-CBN stronger turned into another heavy financial burden for a parent company already struggling to recover from losing its free TV franchise.

Open ABS-CBN’s latest financial report and two main businesses stand out. One makes TV shows, movies, music, and live concerts. The other sells cable TV and home internet subscriptions. Both lost money in the first nine months of 2026, though they face very different problems. Content Production and Distribution—the business behind Batang Quiapo, It’s Showtime, BINI, and Star Cinema—brought in nearly P9 billion in sales, making up more than 85% of ABS-CBN’s total revenue. Still, its costs were higher than its sales, leaving it with a loss of about P2 billion. Meanwhile, the Cable TV and Broadband business—run mainly through Sky Cable Corporation and its subsidiaries—brought in only around P1.6 billion, down 41% from the same period in 2025, while its loss grew to more than P900 million. Source: ABS-CBN’s September 2026 quarterly disclosure.

Sky Cable’s problems go beyond losing subscribers and money. Between 2023 and 2025, ABS-CBN reduced the recorded the value of its Cable and Broadband business by more than P13 billion because those investments were no longer expected to earn what the company originally projected. Meanwhile, Sky Cable’s bank loans still had to be paid back, even as the business meant to pay them grew smaller.

When ABS-CBN’s Channel 2 was the Philippines’ leading free TV network, advertising paid for much of its operations. But ad money rises and falls with the economy since companies spend more when business is good and cut their ad budgets during hard times. Cable television offered something steadier: households paid monthly subscription fees, providing a more regular source of income. Sky Cable also gave ABS-CBN a way to air its own channels, including ANC, Cinema One, Myx, and Lifestyle Network, later renamed Metro.

The Lopez group grew Sky by merging it with other cable companies, including Home Cable in 2004, Destiny Cable, Solid Broadband, and UNI Cable TV in 2012, and internet provider Tri-Isys in 2017. Each acquisition expanded Sky Cable’s reach, but also meant taking on more cables, equipment, and facilities that needed to be maintained and eventually replaced. Sky Cable brought in foreign money as well. Singapore’s STT Communications invested through Sampaquita Communications under deals that later gave it 40% of Sky’s financial returns, while ABS-CBN and related Lopez companies kept the larger share. The arrangements used Philippine Depositary Receipts or PDRs, financial certificates that gave the foreign investor a right to profits linked to shares without directly owning the shares themselves. (READ: FAST FACTS: Other businesses of ABS-CBN)

Sky Cable also borrowed heavily from Philippine banks. Its financial reports list loans from BPI, Security Bank, RCBC, BDO, and other lenders over the years. In 2018 alone, Sky signed a P2-billion BDO loan to finance new equipment and fund projects, plus a separate P762 million loan to pay off an older obligation of Pilipino Cable Corporation, the operator of Home Cable. So, some loans paid for new growth, while other loans simply replaced old debts.

Back then, borrowing was a normal and reasonable way to finance a growing cable business. Laying cables and setting up equipment required huge amounts upfront, while monthly subscription payments trickled in month after month. That business model worked as long as subscribers kept paying long enough for Sky Cable to recover its investment, cover expenses, and pay off the banks. But that plan only worked if Sky Cable’s technology stayed competitive and its subscribers stayed loyal.

Much of Sky Cable’s growth depended on three big technology bets. First, it used its existing cable TV lines to deliver home internet. Instead of replacing every single wire, Sky Cable upgraded parts of the system with fiber-optic lines while keeping older copper-based coaxial cables for the final connection into many homes. Known as “hybrid” network, this was a faster and cheaper way to offer home internet than building a brand new network from scratch.

Second, SkyDirect used satellite dishes to reach households beyond Sky Cable’s wired network. That made sense in an archipelago like the Philippines where running physical cables to every town was far too expensive. This was also one of Sky Cable’s most promising growth businesses. SkyDirect had about one million subscribers in January 2019, barely three years after it was launched, according to ABS-CBN president Carlo Katigbak. By June 2020, Sky reported 1.5 million subscribers nationwide, including families in remote communities beyond the reach of regular TV signals. Satellite technology allowed Sky Cable enter those areas without laying costly cables across islands and provinces.

blocks.caption: The Sky Cable paradox: From ABS-CBN’s second business to its burden

blocks.text: Third, Sky Cable invested in TV set-top boxes that gave subscribers more ways to watch cable channels and, later, streaming apps. By 2019, ABS-CBN’s Cable and Broadband business generated nearly P10 billion in annual revenue and reported a modest profit. The bets seemed to be paying off.
Between 2020 and 2024, four major setbacks derailed Sky Cable’s growth:

items: The June 30, 2020 NTC shutdown of SkyDirect, which ended a fast-growing satellite TV business.
The rise of online streaming, which reduced demand for traditional cable subscriptions.
The race to bring fiber internet directly into homes, which exposed the limits of Sky Cable’s older network.
The canceled P6.75-billion sale to PLDT, which left ABS-CBN with a business it had already prepared to sell.

blocks.text: The shutdown of SkyDirect. On May 5, 2020, the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) ordered ABS-CBN’s free TV and radio stations off the air after its broadcast franchise expired. On June 30, the regulator issued another order shutting SkyDirect and ABS-CBN TVplus, citing the expiration of the permits they operated under.

blocks.caption: Screenshot from ABS-CBN X posted on June 30, 2020

blocks.text: For Sky Cable, the shutdown was particularly damaging because SkyDirect was still attracting subscribers fast. From one million subscribers in January 2019, it had jumped to 1.5 million by June 2020. These were households paying monthly bills, or buying prepaid credits, to watch via satellite dishes. The service was especially useful in provincial areas where laying cable lines would have cost too much. Sky Cable had found a smart way to grow beyond the towns and cities covered by its existing wires, and that business was still booming when the government ordered it to stop. The order also required Sky Cable to refund unused prepaid credits, advance payments, and deposits.

The first two weakened Sky Cable’s TV business. The third showed the high cost of relying on an older broadband network while rivals built newer ones. The fourth deprived ABS-CBN of an opportunity to sell the company and use the proceeds for its other pressing financial needs.
The shutdown deprived Sky Cable of another major income source for ABS-CBN, and a fast-growing subscription business before its full commercial potential could be realized.

The shift to streaming. Netflix, YouTube, and other online apps offered programs that viewers could watch whenever, wherever they wanted, without paying for a traditional cable package. Sky Cable tried to fight back by launching SKY EVO in 2021, an Android-based TV box combining cable channels with streaming apps. But smart TVs, smartphones, and tablets were already letting people stream online entertainment without needing a cable subscription at all. SKY EVO was an attempt to adapt, but it could not stop the massive shift in viewing habits. (READ: Streaming services ‘winning hearts and minds’ of Filipinos, says new study)

The race for home internet. As cable TV subscribers left, Sky Cable needed broadband to become a stronger business. But rivals PLDT, Globe, and Converge ICT were pouring billions into “fiber-to-the-home” networks, which run pure fiber optic cables straight into customers houses and offices. Sky Cable’s older hybrid network could deliver fast download speeds, but traditional cable wires generally had less capacity for uploads, such as sending large files or joining video calls, and could slow down when too many neighbors went online at once.

These differences became more obvious during the pandemic, when families relied on home internet for work, online classes, video meetings, gaming, and streaming. Pure fiber networks offered much better upload speeds and room to handle heavy traffic. Sky Cable had made a technology bet that no longer fit the market. Extending the life of its older cable wires had saved money at first, but maintaining and upgrading that aging system grew more expensive just as rivals were building faster, brand new fiber networks. Sky Cable’s technology had not stopped working, but its earlier cost savings were no longer enough to keep up.

The aborted PLDT exit. In March 2023, ABS-CBN and other Sky shareholders agreed to sell the whole company to PLDT for P6.75 billion. The Philippine Competition Commission cleared the transaction in January 2024. Sky had already announced plans to discontinue cable television in February and focus strictly on broadband. Before that happened, however, both sides called off the deal because certain conditions had not been met and they could not agree on revised terms. Sky Cable kept running its cable TV service, which ABS-CBN remained responsible for a business it had already prepared to hand over.
The financial consequences from these setbacks became harder and harder to handle. Sky Cable was losing subscribers and revenue, yet its bank loans still had to be paid.

Sky Cable’s money problems appeared in two ways: It was losing money from operations, and some of the businesses and equipment it had acquired were worth less than the amounts recorded in its books. When a company buys another business, for example, it may pay extra because it expects future income from customers and a well-known brand. Accountants call this additional value goodwill. If the expected future income are no longer realistic, the company must slash that recovered value.

In 2023, ABS-CBN reduced Sky’s recorded goodwill by about P4.5 billion and lowered the value of customer accounts and other non-physical assets by nearly P1.9 billion. More cuts followed for equipment and other property. Between 2023 and 2025, the Cable and Broadband business recorded over P13 billion in these value reductions, known as impairment charges. They were accounting losses rather than cash spent during those years, but they showed that Sky Cable’s past investments would never deliver the returns ABS-CBN once expected.
The decline in the business was equally striking.
Sources: ABS-CBN annual reports and September 2026 quarterly disclosures. The massive losses in 2023 and 2024 included major cuts in asset values.
Annual revenue fell by roughly two-thirds between 2019 and 2025. Even after slashing costs, Sky Cable kept losing money.

Its debts became another major headache. By the end of 2023, Sky owed about P4.5 billion in bank loans. Because its finances were weakening, Sky Cable struggled to meet strict conditions written into those loan agreements. As a result, those loans had to be listed as short-term obligations in its financial reports, meaning the Sky Cable no longer had the automatic right to put off payments. That did not necessarily mean the banks were demanding immediate payment, but it showed how serious Sky’s borrowing problem had become.

By the end of 2025, Sky had approximately P9 billion in assets but owed around P10 billion in bank loans, unpaid bills, and other debts, meaning what it owed was roughly P1 billion more than everything it owed. ABS-CBN itself was also struggling. By September 2026, the group had nearly P12 billion in total loans and had racked up around P750 million in interest and related borrowing costs over nine months. Sky Cable was part of that debt load, while ABS-CBN’s content business was also losing money. Its auditors warned that the group’s continuing losses and money pressures created serious doubt about whether it could keep operating and paying its bills.

In July 2024, Sky Cable made a major change in its technology strategy. Instead of spending heavily to upgrade its aging cable network, it signed a deal to use Converge ICT’s fiber optic infrastructure in Metro Manila. Converge was one of the very rivals Sky Cable had been fighting for broadband customers. Under the deal, Sky Cable could use Converge’s network to offer modern fiber connections to its own subscribers, avoiding the full cost of building those connections itself. (READ: Why Converge thinks it’s the next big thing in telco)

blocks.caption: SCALING UP. Converge CEO and co-founder Dennis Anthony Uy speaks at the launch of the DTI AI and Scale-up Center.

blocks.text: The partnership gave Sky Cable a practical way to stay in the game, yet it also showed how much its strategy had changed. A company that spent decades building and upgrading its own cable network was now relying on a competitor’s infrastructure to give customers what they wanted.

blocks.caption: Screenshot from Sky Cable Corp. statement on July 22, 2024.

blocks.text: Sky also needed breathing room from its banks. In February 2025, BDO, BPI, RCBC, and Security Bank agreed to change the repayment terms of P4.25 billion in loans, pushing some deadlines as far as 2032. The deal gave Sky Cable more time to pay and eased some of the financial conditions it had to meet. But the loans were not forgiven.

The debt deal produced an unusual result in Sky Cable’s 2025 financial report: an accounting gain of about P1.4 billion, even though no actual cash entered Sky Cable’s bank account. That gain came from how accountants recalculated the value of the loans after their terms changed. It helped shrink Sky’s reported loss for 2025, but the business still had to pay back every peso under the new schedule.

The financial troubles of Sky Cable came up again when ABS-CBN brought in new investors in 2026. In August, the media company announced a P6 billion investment deal: P3.5 billion from I&C Holdings, P2.2 billion from three Lopez family investment companies, and P300 million from Lopez Inc. The fresh cash is meant to support operations, pay overdue bills, and cut down bank debt.

blocks.caption: After Gabby sold to Ramon Ang, Piki Lopez is securing the family’s crown jewels

blocks.text: But I&C, the largest new investor, wanted protection from some of ABS-CBN’s existing money troubles. Under the agreement, ABS-CBN promised to pay for any Sky Cable worker separation costs above ₱402 million, along with certain other Sky-related bills. I&C also required that any updates to ABS-CBN’s loans with BPI and UnionBank leave the network with terms at least as good as before. Simply put, the new investor wanted a guarantee that renegotiating those bank loans wouldn’t leave ABS-CBN in a worse financial spot.

On top of that, I&C demanded protection from other identified losses worth over P3 billion. The message was unmistakable: I&C was ready to invest, but only with strict guardrails against ABS-CBN’s existing risks. Even so, those guardrails didn’t erase Sky’s debts, and they didn’t mean ABS-CBN was planning to sell or close Sky down.

That detail matters. I&C was not refusing to touch any risk connected to Sky Cable, and the P402-million threshold was not a cap on everything ABS-CBN might still have to spend on the subsidiary. Rather, the investor wanted legal protection from specific liabilities. In business, this is known as ring-fencing: drawing clear boundaries around certain financial risks so they do not automatically become an unlimited obligation for the new investor.

For ABS-CBN, this meant Sky’s financial problems were no longer just a matter of managing a troubled subsidiary. They had become a key bargaining chip in bringing fresh money into the parent company. The investment deal did not establish that Sky would be sold, closed, or separated from ABS-CBN, but it showed that Sky’s lingering debts were serious enough for a new investor to demand protection.

Sky Cable’s story shows how a company can borrow and invest in technologies that make total commercial and financial sense at the time, only to find out later that the market has moved in another direction. Its hybrid cable network fell behind newer fiber internet, its satellite TV business was shut down by regulators, and its attempt to modernize cable TV could not stop the shift to streaming. Those technology bets lost much of their expected value, yet the debts they created remained.

Sky Cable is now trying to survive by renting space on a rival’s network and taking more time to pay its banks. Neither move guarantees that lost customers will come back or that the business will make a profit again.

Sky Cable once gave ABS-CBN a way to earn steady money outside of free TV. Almost four decades later, the question has reversed: Can Sky Cable become financially strong enough to stop depending on the company it was supposed to help? – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

articles.title: Duterte camp opposes closed-door testimonies for ICC witnesses
articles.summary: The defense team of former president Rodrigo Duterte has opposed the International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecution's request for several witnesses to testify behind closed doors, saying the sweeping…

blocks.text: November 24, 2026 | 10:09am

MANILA, Philippines — The defense team of former president Rodrigo Duterte has opposed the International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecution's request for several witnesses to testify behind closed doors, saying the sweeping use of such measures would undermine the public nature of the trial.

In an 11-page filing dated November 23, Duterte's counsel Peter Haynes and his team questioned the prosecution's request to keep most of its witnesses anonymous, saying it failed to establish that each witness faced an objectively justifiable risk.

The prosecution is seeking anonymity for 55 of its 69 witnesses, including 32 insiders. It also wants 22 witnesses to testify entirely in closed sessions, according to the defense's redacted submission.
"Simply put, the Prosecution is requesting anonymity for 79% of its testifying witnesses, 40% of whom would then give evidence effectively in secret," the defense said.

The defense argued that the extent of the requested measures would infringe on Duterte's right to a public trial, saying public scrutiny should not be a reason to keep testimonies away from public view.
"Contrary to the Prosecution's assertions, heightened public scrutiny and interest are not grounds to set aside the right to a public trial," the defense said.

"A public trial is, by its design, meant to ensure a fair trial, and foster trust and confidences in the genuine process of justice. That is not achieved when in-court evidence is given behind closed doors or by faceless witnesses with distorted voices," it added.

It also questioned the prosecution's basis for seeking witness protection, saying factors such as a witness' public profile, increased media exposure, membership in the Philippine National Police (PNP) or government, residence in the Philippines or familiarity with Duterte were insufficient grounds for granting protective measures.
The defense said the prosecution had failed to establish that the same objectively justifiable risks applied to each witness in the categories for which protection was being sought.
It also raised concerns over the extent of evidence that would be withheld from public view if the request were granted.

According to the filing, the prosecution is seeking to anonymize all in-court evidence involving 46 charged incidents, leaving identifiable evidence for only 10 incidents, and even then, only partially.

The defense said the proposed public testimony for nine of the 10 incidents would rely on four witnesses whose evidence was "confined to second hand information and/or the aftermaths of the alleged killings."
"Anonymising evidence so extensive yet so determinative of the case is incompatible with the principles of publicity and transparency in this trial," the defense said.

The defense maintained that it does not oppose private sessions when the prosecution can establish that witnesses face objectively justifiable risks and that their answers may reveal their identities.
However, it objected to the request to place 22 witnesses under entirely closed sessions, saying less restrictive measures could address the alleged risks.
The defense proposed the targeted use of private sessions, along with pseudonyms and face and voice distortions, instead of withholding entire testimonies from the public.
It also argued that witness anonymity could affect the ICC's ability to establish the truth, as public testimony allows people to scrutinize the credibility and reliability of witnesses.

"Public anonymity may affect the ability of the Chamber to fulfill its truth-seeking mandate, as making a witness's identity known to the public increases their commitment to tell the truth as well as their feeling of public accountability," the defense said.
It added that keeping allegations hidden would deprive the defense of information from the public that could help challenge witness accounts.
"If the allegations are all kept hidden from public view, the Defence loses one of the most important tools in its investigative arsenal; allegations being made in full view of the public," it said.
The defense also opposed the prosecution's request for special measures for an unnamed witness, saying there was no basis to consider the individual vulnerable.
"There is no reason to believe [REDACTED] is a vulnerable witness," the defense said.

In its concluding requests, the defense asked the ICC Trial Chamber III to consider the proportionate use of pseudonyms and face and voice distortions, reject requests for entirely closed sessions for certain witnesses, and decide on private sessions on a case-by-case basis.

The filing comes ahead of the scheduled opening of Duterte's ICC trial on November 30. He is facing three counts of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder over killings allegedly committed in the Philippines between Nov. 1, 2011 and March 16, 2019, as part of his administration's war on drugs.

articles.title: Alleged Tumbler Ridge shooting co-conspirator asks court to revoke detention order
articles.summary: According to court filings, Melody Bryant was not the only one who initially failed to recognize killer Jesse Van Rootselaar was "genuinely dangerous." The motion says records show the shooter shared…

image.caption: Melody Bryant, who was charged under the name James Cody Bryant in October, is seen in a court sketch. The alleged co-conspirator of Tumbler Ridge school shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar has applied to revoke a U.S. detention order. (Lois Silver)

blocks.text: An American accused of helping Jesse Van Rootselaar plan the Tumbler Ridge massacre has filed an application to get out of jail, asking a Seattle court judge to review and revoke a previous detention order.

A magistrate judge ordered the detention of Melody Bryant, who was charged under the name James Cody Bryant in October, after the government argued the accused would be a danger to the public if released.
Bryant, 30, is charged with conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country, an offence that carries a maximum sentence of life in prison and a $250,000 US fine. She has pleaded not guilty.
The trial was originally scheduled to begin next month, but has been moved to December 2027.

Her lawyers say in court filings that their client is not a danger to the public and should be released with conditions. They say at the time of the Oct. 13 detention hearing, they had not yet received discovery documents and could not properly respond to the government's argument.
U.S. resident allegedly gave advice, money to Tumbler Ridge shooter
On Feb. 10, Van Rootselaar shot and killed her mother Jennifer Strang, 39, and half-brother Emmett Jacobs, 11, in their home.

She then drove to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School where she gunned down Abel Mwansa, 12, Zoey Benoit, 12, Ezekiel Schofield, 13, Kylie Smith, 12, Ticaria Lampert, 12, and educational assistant Shannda Aviugana-Durand, 39.
Two other students were shot but survived.

items: Alleged co-conspirator in Tumbler Ridge shooting has trial delayed until December 2027

blocks.text: In their 33-page motion for revocation of detention order filed last week, Bryant's lawyers say the case is based mainly on nearly 74,000 individual texts between Van Rootselaar and Bryant on messaging platform Discord, sent between Aug. 1 and Feb. 10, 2025.
Approximately two-thirds of those messages, numbering 47,750, are from Van Rootselaar to Bryant.
Bryant's lawyers say while some of their clients messages "may be tasteless and, in retrospect, were ill considered" they are protected by the First Amendment.

"For better or worse, the First Amendment also protects their debate about whether a school shooting or attack on a crowd would be more likely to make someone infamous, even if the government tries to recast that conversation as 'tactical advice,'" said the Nov. 18 motion filed by Bryant's lawyers.
Discord messages reveal Tumbler Ridge shooter, U.S. resident planning attack
The motion includes excerpts of chats between Bryant and Van Rootselaar, including one on Christmas Day 2025 used to show instances where Bryant refused to engage in violent rants.
"I hope I ruin everyone's life when I do my plan. I want nobody to recover … whenever I say some mentally ill ahh stuff I feel like u stop messaging me lol…," wrote Van Rootselaar.
Bryant wrote back, "Harder to reply to."
The court filings say, for part of the six-month period where Bryant spoke daily to Van Rootselaar, the shooter's "plan" was clearly a fantasy because Van Rootselaar did not have access to guns.
"Eventually, however, the RCMP returned her seized weapons."
Seized guns used in shooting: documents

According to the court filings, Bryant was not the only one who initially failed to recognize Van Rootselaar was "genuinely dangerous." The motion says records show the shooter shared her plans widely and had even "received encouragement from other online contacts."
She got tactical advice from ChatGPT, family and friends bought her ammunition, even after she was released from psychiatric hospitalization and the RCMP, according to the motion.

items: Tumbler Ridge shooter stole guns from family safe as part of attack plans, new court filings reveal
RCMP says it still won't share more details on firearms used in Tumbler Ridge shooting

blocks.text: Bryant's lawyers add that the RCMP had removed, and then later returned, Van Rootselaar's guns, "one of which had been altered to enable more rapid firing."
"In fact, the RCMP apparently returned the gun with the alteration intact. Van Rootselaar then used the altered firearm in the shooting," said the Nov. 18 motion.

Days after the Tumbler Ridge shooting, RCMP said a long gun and modified rifle were seized from the school, and two firearms including a shotgun were seized among a number of other firearms at the residence.

The shotgun is believed to have been used in the homicides at the home and had not been previously seized by police. Mounties also said they had not previously seized the main firearm used in the school shooting and its origins are unknown.
Report details Tumbler Ridge shooter’s alleged ChatGPT interactions
Bryant's lawyers say their client promised not to snitch on the shooter because Bryant believed it would result in violence, and accelerate the shooter's homicidal plans.

"While it is horrifying in retrospect to imagine that Ms. Bryant might have stopped Van Rootselaar from committing a terrible crime if she had contacted the police, it is undisputed that the law provided no affirmative duty to do so," said the motion.
The court filings said in the past Bryant was able to talk Van Rootselaar out of committing a crime, and did not understand violence was imminent.
A memorial for the victims of a school shooting at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School is pictured on Feb. 11, 2026. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
Bryant's lawyers say the shooter viewed Bryant as "a nonjudgemental sounding board for ruminating about her mental illness," and that Bryant helped her resist her urges.
The defence included chats to illustrate that.
In an undated message, Van Rootselaar writes "I **really** wanna shoot ppl, idk what to do with that feeling lmao. Like how do I relieve that? I can't talk about it much even."
"Yeah I think most would snitch," replies Bryant.
"Except for you who silently discourage it and a few others who openly encourage it," responds Van Rootselaar.
Government distorted evidence: defence

Bryant's lawyers say the U.S. government's 41-page complaint against their client is "replete with distortions" and includes rearranged text messages made to appear that Bryant was agreeing to help the shooter build a bomb.

The motion for revocation of detention order says the conversation included in the complaint showing Bryant agreeing to pay for a lighter needed to make a bomb occurred over two days and in between 225 messages.

"In fact, nowhere in the complete chats does Van Rootselaar say that she needs a lighter for the bomb. Nowhere does Bryant offer to provide Van Rootselaar a lighter for that purpose," said the court filing.
U.S. resident met Tumbler Ridge shooter on Omegle: FBI
Bryant's lawyers say the decision to piece the texts together "seems designed to lead the magistrate judge to make a false inference."
They say while Bryant agreed to watch a livestream and if possible distribute it, she did not agree with Van Rootselaar's plans to kill people.
The motion says the fact that law enforcement left Bryant in the community for seven months after reviewing her Discord chats shows she does not pose a danger.
The magistrate judge concluded Bryant suffers from a "deeply rooted" mental illness and substance abuse history.

Bryant's lawyers say that is not true. Bryant is currently being treated for gender dysphoria and had previously been prescribed medication for anxiety but no longer takes that drug, according to the motion.
The U.S. state's attorney's response is due Wednesday, then a judge will decide if Bryant should be released.

articles.title: US adds Megaspeed, AI firm at center of Nvidia scandal, to trade blacklist
articles.summary:
Singapore-based company entangled in scandal over alleged spy Alice Huang’s affair with Jensen Huang

The US commerce department published

blocks.text: The US commerce department published an official notice on Monday adding the Singapore-based company Megaspeed, and its subsidiaries in Thailand and Malaysia, to a trade blacklist.

Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner which has been under investigation by US authorities since 2024 over whether it diverted AI chips to China, will now need approval from the commerce department to obtain US exports, which is likely to be denied.

The expected addition of the company follows revelations that the recently reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a ⁠relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman and Megaspeed’s controlling shareholder, who is reportedly alleged to be a ⁠spy for Beijing. China has said the spy accusations are “groundless”.
“The Department of Commerce still needs to explain to Congress why this took so long,” Senator Pete Ricketts, a Nebraska Republican, said in a social media post.

The New York Times reported on Monday that Alice Huang “kept in contact with an official of China’s top spy agency for more than a year while she was carrying out a secret affair with Jensen Huang, according to multiple people with knowledge of US intelligence reports that describe the encounters”.
The US justice department is investigating whether Megaspeed violated US export controls by shipping Nvidia chips to China.
Megaspeed did not immediately return a request for comment. A week ago, the company issued a statement saying it conducts legitimate and lawful business, including complying with US export controls.
It also said Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed in August 2025.
Nvidia has said it recently formed an export control committee to oversee trade compliance and national security risks.

As Semafor notes, the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, has been under pressure to act since the news of Jensen Huang’s relationship with the former reproter for Chinese state television who became a director at Singapore-based Megaspeed in 2023 became public.

The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said earlier this month that his agency along with the Pentagon, the state department and the US trade representative’s office had all wanted Megaspeed on the blacklist “for months” but that “Commerce holds the pen”.
After the news broke, treasury secretary Scott Bessent publicly complained that the commerce department had not yet placed the company on its entity list.

He also called out Nvidia. “The real story here should be: did Nvidia know their client and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” Bessent told CNBC’s Squawk Box program.

The US justice department and commerce department issued a joint statement last week saying they would “bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred”.
Reuters contributed reporting

articles.title: What does the proposed Pax Silica bill in the House contain?
articles.summary: A House bill in the early stages seeks to provide the framework on how to manage the planned semiconductor hub

blocks.text: Graphics by Nico Villarete/Rappler
A House bill in the early stages seeks to provide the framework on how to manage the planned semiconductor hub

items: During President Trump's visit to the Philippines, no Pax Silica agreement was signed, but House lawmakers are proposing legislation to support an AI-native industrial hub in New Clark City.

House Bill No. 11758 aims to establish an Advanced Industries Zone and the Advanced Industries Development Authority (AIDA), which would oversee operations and provide incentives for qualified enterprises in high-tech industries.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
When US President Donald Trump visited the Philippines during the ASEAN Summit, he signed no Pax Silica agreement with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

But even as major hurdles hound a possible deal, administration-allied House lawmakers are ready to supplement a Pax Silica initiative with a bill clearing the bureaucratic and legal obstacles to an AI-native industrial acceleration hub in New Clark City in Capas, Tarlac.
House Bill No. 11758, filed in October by six congressmen led by Deputy Speaker Ronnie Puno, is called the Advanced Industries Development Act.
The bill seeks to create an Advanced Industries Zone, as well as its independent government body called the Advanced Industries Development Authority (AIDA).
The Zone is envisaged to be “decentralized, self-reliant, and self-sustaining…with minimum government intervention.”
The AIDA, meanwhile, would be run by a board, composed of 11 governors, including a chairperson appointed by the President.

Based on the proposal, the AIDA would be tasked to administer the Zone and oversee persons and entities with projects in it. They would fix and collect fees, enter into contracts, and have an authorized capital of P50 billion.
If it becomes law, the AIDA would effectively be given a 25-year, renewable, franchise “to construct, operate, and maintain systems for power and water distribution within the Zone.”

Under the proposal, a person or an entity (called a locator) can apply for certification as a qualified enterprise with AIDA’s board of governors. This would allow them to do business within the Zone.
But to be a qualified enterprise, they must meet the minimum investment capital worth P15 billion, excluding land value.
Their enterprise must belong to any of the following high-tech industries:

items: semiconductor design, fabrication, assembly, testing, or packaging
advanced manufacturing (automation, robotics, precision engineering, or advanced materials)
data centers and computing infrastructure for AI computing
processing of critical minerals and specialty materials
scientific research, development, and technology commercialization
energy facilities

blocks.text: Marcos previously said the Philippine development under the Pax Silica initiative would include the construction of data centers, an issue that is at the heart of environmental groups’ opposition.
Based on the proposal, qualified enterprises would enjoy exclusive financial incentives and operational privileges for their projects within the zone. These include:

items: income tax holiday for seven years from the start of project’s commercial operations
special corporate income tax or enhanced deductions regime in lieu of or upon the expiration of the income tax holiday
exemptions from value-added tax and customs duty

blocks.text: The Pax Silica initiative has been met with intense pushback in the Philippines amid fears that hundreds of indigenous peoples and farmers in Tarlac province would be displaced.
The House bill explicitly excludes ancestral lands from being declared alienable and disposable.

Human Rights Watch said Aeta comunities in Capas have been seeking recognition of their ancestral domain since the 1990s, but have yet to receive the title. The IPs have been informed by the government that their homes and land would be affected by the Pax Silica project, and that they would be relocated by December.

The House bill gives preferential hiring to Capas residents, members of IP communities whose ancestral domains are within or adjacent to the Zone, and potentially displaced persons due to the project.

blocks.caption: [OPINION] Pax Silica and the erasure of Ayta Hungey ancestral lands

blocks.text: HB 11758, whose other authors include congressmen Miguel Luis Villafuerte, Albert Garcia, Alfredo Maranon III, Rolando Valeriano, and Jolo Revilla, is in the early stages of the legislative process.
It has been referred to the economic affairs committee, but has yet to be tackled.

As with many bills, this proposal could gain further traction if backed by the House leadership — or if House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos or House Speaker Bojie Dy files their own version of the measure.
So far, the bill is not yet a Palace priority measure, and has no counterpart in the Senate. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Chinese vessels in West PH Sea increased to 48 after ASEAN Summit 2026 --AFP
articles.summary: The number of Chinese vessels monitored in the West Philippine Sea increased to 48 in the past week following the ASEAN Summit 2026, the Armed Forces of the Philippines said on Tuesday.

blocks.text: Published November 24, 2026 9:29am
The number of Chinese vessels monitored in the West Philippine Sea (WPS) increased to 48 in the past week following the ASEAN Summit 2026, the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) said on Tuesday.

Interviewed on Super Radyo dzBB, AFP spokesperson for the WPS (ret.) Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad said 48 Chinese vessels were recorded from November 17 to 23. This was higher compared to the 19 Chinese vessels recorded from November 9 to 16.
“Noong ASEAN (Summit), nagpakita sila na kaunti na ang nilagay nila sa ating EEZ na mga barko,” Trinidad said.
(During ASEAN [Summit], they showed that they have deployed just a few ships in our EEZ.)
Trinidad said the Philippines continues its efforts to monitor foreign vessels in its maritime domain through its sea-based, air-based, land-based, and space-based monitoring capabilities.
He also cited the contributions of civilian maritime auxiliaries, particularly Filipino fisherfolk and seafarers, who provide photographs, videos, and reports of foreign vessel movements.
Trinidad said the information provided by civilians supplements the military's monitoring capabilities, allowing the Philippines to know almost in real time when foreign vessels enter its waters.

Tensions continue as Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea, a conduit for more than $3 trillion of annual shipborne commerce, including parts claimed by the Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei.
Parts of the South China Sea that fall within Philippine territory have been renamed by the government as West Philippine Sea to reinforce the country’s claim.

The West Philippine Sea refers to the maritime areas on the western side of the Philippine archipelago including Luzon Sea and the waters around, within and adjacent to the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.
In 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines over China's claims in the South China Sea, saying that it had "no legal basis."
China has refused to recognize the decision. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon chose ‘long walk’ to witness box rather than silence, his barrister tells court
articles.summary:
Former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murders of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Baird’s Paddington home in February 2024

  • Get our

blocks.text: Beau Lamarre-Condon could have sat in silence and let the crown “do its worst”, but he made the choice to take the “long walk” to the witness box, a jury has been told.
Lamarre-Condon is accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird and his partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.
The former officer has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
His barrister John Stratton SC urged the jury to accept Lamarre-Condon’s testimony as truthful, as he wrapped up his closing statement on Tuesday morning.
“He didn’t have to give evidence. He could have said to the crown, ‘Do your worst but I’m not going to help you’,” Stratton told the New South Wales supreme court.
“He didn’t do that.
“He took that long walk to the witness box, and he did it voluntarily and he subjected himself to a detailed, fierce cross-examination by a very experienced crown prosecutor that went over six days.”
Stratton claimed the cross-examination did not break down his client, nor did it establish he was telling new lies.
“The fact the accused has chosen to give evidence does not mean he needs to prove his case … the onus of proof is always on the crown,” he said.
The double murder trial is expected to wrap up in the coming days, with the jury soon set to begin deliberations.
Justice Natalie Adams will spend the afternoon giving her instructions to the jurors.

Video edited by Mabel Pickering

articles.title: Nvidia reinstates CEO Jensen Huang after affair with alleged spy as Trump says 'I made the deal'
articles.summary: Nvidia had come under pressure from President Trump to reappoint Huang, whose comeback helped add $1tn to the company's stock value.

blocks.text: The head of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI told the BBC that the Nvidia board must have been under "enormous pressure" from the White House to reinstate Huang.
Prof Stuart Russell, who is professor of computer science at UC Berkeley, said the stock price of Nvidia and similar firms has been a major factor in "underpinning US economic growth for years".
"I assume the White House was worried that the markets would go down a lot further in the next few weeks unless they go him back in," he says.
Trump's vocal backing of Huang comes despite the concerns of US lawmakers, including some Republicans, over the CEO's affair and Nvidia's compliance with US export controls.
"Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang," Republican congressman Don Bacon of Nebraska said.
"We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible."
Sen Tom Cotton, fellow Republican who represents Arkansas, vowed that Congress would investigate.
"The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back," he said.
Democrats, who will control both chambers of Congress from January, have already promised to launch Nvidia investigations.
Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is set to be chairwoman of the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement that the reinstatement was "reckless".

Congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a member of the House foreign affairs committee, also condemned the move in a statement to the BBC as "premature" before multiple investigations are concluded. Fellow Democratic Representative Andre Carson, a member of the House intelligence committee, told the BBC that "Congress needs a full accounting of whether any controlled technology was diverted" to China.
Huang is scheduled to appear before Congress for a closed-door interview with three House committees on 1 December.
Two days later, he has been asked to testify before the Senate banking committee.

Since returning last year to the White House, Trump has amassed a significant level of investment in Nvidia. Recent financial disclosures show he purchased $265,000 in its stock and sold as much as $15,000 worth of shares in September.

A BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the last two years shows he purchased shares of Nvidia stock worth between $23m and $86m (£18m and £66m). And he has bought Nvidia stock 85 separate times through a number of investment accounts.
The value of those holdings would have been affected by the recent fall in Nvidia's stock price amid Huang's exit.
Trump has also sold some of his stake in Nvidia since returning to the presidency. Over 19 sales, Trump gained between $3.5m and $10.2m, according to his government disclosures.
The BBC has contacted the White House.

Both Trump and White House have repeatedly rejected assertions that he has profited from the presidency. The president has said "everybody" was making money from rising stocks and he does not make decisions related to his investment accounts.
The White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.
With additional reporting from Brandon Drenon and Rachel Clun

The Samahang Manibela, Mananakay, at Nagkaisang Terminal ng Transportasyon (MANIBELA) will continue its transport strike until Wednesday, November 25, its leader said Tuesday.
“Hanggang bukas, sasalubungin natin. Wala tayong biyahe. Magmamartsa na tayo papunta roon,” MANIBELA chairperson Mar Valbuena said in a video posted on the group’s Facebook page.

MANIBELA on Tuesday staged its second day of protest near the Malacañang gate in Nagtahan, Manila.
Valbuena said participating jeepney drivers would remain off the roads as they protest what he described as the appointment of alleged corrupt officials to government positions.

He criticized alleged corruption and irregularities involving the Land Transportation Office (LTO), including transactions involving Dermalog and Paynamics, as well as alleged excessive fees, kickbacks, and payolas.
Members from different MANIBELA chapters had gathered in Nagtahan to bring their concerns to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
After holding a program in the area, the group planned to march toward the LTO office to continue its protest.
