articles.title: At AI speed, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang finds exoneration
articles.summary: (1st UPDATE) Huang is scheduled to testify before Congress regarding his ties to a woman accused of being a Chinese spy, amids calls for legislation to prevent AI technology from reaching China

blocks.text: SAN FRANCISCO, USA – In the AI era, everything moves fast.

Jensen Huang’s 11-day transformation from persona non grata to prodigal emperor happened before Nvidia began in earnest its investigation into myriad allegations against him, including the executive’s extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese asset. Reuters could not confirm Alice Huang’s affiliation with the Chinese government.

Few parallels exist. Walt Disney’s Bob Iger retired in 2020 but came back just two years later before leaving again earlier this year. Among tech firm founders, only Zynga’s Mark Pincus and Workday’s Aneel Bhusri, who both spent about two years away as CEOs, come anywhere close. Steve Jobs spent a dozen years away from Apple . OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s whiplash return from exile in five days in 2023 is an exception.

But none of them were shrouded in as much scandal as Huang’s dizzying fall and rapid exoneration, which came after allegations of multiple affairs, including with subordinates and an executive for a key customer.

blocks.caption: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO

blocks.text: The Nvidia board vowed not to reinstate him as recently as Tuesday. But amid pressure from shareholders, venture capitalists and President Donald Trump, Nvidia announced early Monday Huang would once again control the company.
The shares jumped as much as 32% on Monday, November 23.

Huang’s initial downfall stemmed from revelations he had a lengthy affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who was a director of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company. In the fallout, Reuters reported he had had affairs with two staffers, causing the board to lose confidence in the 63-year-old CEO. He was replaced by Nvidia CFO Colette Kress while the company searched for a permanent successor.

Among the shortlist of candidates, the board reached out, according to reports, to Rene Haas, CEO of Arm O9Ty.F, which at 7 a.m. ET (1200 GMT) announced it had extended its contract with Haas through 2033.
Within two hours, Nvidia announced Huang’s return.

With Nvidia seen as a critical piece of the AI economy, industry executives circled the wagons around the fallen CEO, including on social media and in urgent calls to the board of directors, according to media reports, as Nvidia lost about $1 trillion in market value, casting doubt on the AI trade that had boosted global markets over four years.

University of Washington professor Margaret O’Mara, who writes about the history of technology, said the norm in Silicon Valley has often been to “let this indispensable man do his innovative stuff” and let misbehavior slide. “You can be a brilliant jerk if you can get things done,” she said.
Reaction to Jensen Huang’s return was swift.

In addition to Wall Street’s elation, Trump praised the board for having “made the correct and proper decision” while taking credit for its U-turn. Elon Musk said on X that “the mistake has been corrected,” and venture capitalists like Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner celebrated the move on social media.

Criticizing the move were elected officials on both sides of the aisle. Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts said it was “reckless” and the Nvidia board still owed Congress answers about the company’s compliance with US export controls. Republican Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska said Nvidia’s leadership ought to have ignored the Trump administration’s “inexplicable desire to save Huang.”

Meanwhile, Nvidia is facing a shareholder suit alleging the company ⁠and Huang defrauded shareholders ​by concealing Huang’s alleged relationship with Alice Huang. And Reuters reported exclusively last week that Huang misled several of the company’s leaders, including its general counsel, about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang.
Huang had apologized for his behavior in an email to Nvidia staff saying, “My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do.”

His return contrasts with traditional accountability in corporate America where inter-office affairs with subordinates are disqualifying. Consider the fate of the CEOs of Nestle, BP, Norfolk Southern and Kohl’s, who in just the past three years were all pushed out for inappropriate workplace relationships.

“Accepting the resignation was right,” said Nada Kakbadse, Henley Business School professor of corporate governance and ethics, referring to Nvidia. “A relationship with a direct report, plus reports that he misled the general counsel, is a code-of-conduct problem and not a private matter. The reinstatement is the weak decision.”

Yet, Nvidia is viewed in Washington as critical to the advancement of AI, making Huang’s purgatory, like AI itself, rapid. The Trump administration moved quickly, playing a singular role in Huang’s return.
Trump and Vice President JD Vance over the weekend were personally engaged with Nvidia’s board to pressure them to reinstate Huang, people familiar with the matter told Reuters.

US Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also played roles in determining Jensen Huang was not a security risk to the US and did not see any evidence that he did anything illegal or untoward related to US national security, these people said.

In conversations over the weekend, administration and White House officials debated whether there could be a national security crisis because he personally held relationships with supply chain companies deemed critical, one of the people said.
The Nvidia CEO, the White House said, had been unaware that Alice Huang had any affiliations with the Chinese state, one person told Reuters.

So, despite its assurances that it would seek a new leader, the Nvidia board reversed its decision and announced his reinstatement Monday morning. “Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA,” said board chairman Harvey Jones.
Huang returned to Nvidia’s Silicon Valley headquarters Monday to cheers from staffers, who chanted his name. “I’m terribly sorry for putting all of you all through all of this,” he said.

US lawmakers from both parties sharply criticized Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Huang, saying Congress should tighten restrictions on China’s access to the company’s advanced AI chips and scrutinize the circumstances surrounding Huang’s return.

Senate intelligence committee chairman Tom Cotton, a Republican, on Monday,called on Congress to pass the Chip Security Act, a bill that seeks to address legally exported advanced chips later being diverted to China, where their sales are restricted.
The bill would require chipmakers to track the location of advanced AI processors and notify the government if they suspect chips have reached prohibited users.
For Nvidia, the measure could create new compliance costs and reporting obligations.

Democratic US Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who is set to chair the Banking Committee starting in January, called the decision to reinstate Huang “reckless,” adding Nvidia’s board still owes Congress answers about the company’s compliance with US export controls. The Banking Committee is responsible for approving legislation on export controls.

“Jensen Huang’s return only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure Nvidia does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk,” Warren said.

Huang will testify on December 3 before the US Senate banking committee in a public hearing, the panel’s Republican Chair Tim Scott said Monday, as lawmakers probe allegations about ⁠Huang’s ties to a woman accused ​of being a Chinese spy. Huang’s personal spokesperson declined to comment on the planned appearance.

Republican Senator Pete Ricketts, a member of the Senate banking committee, said in a statement on Monday that the Nvidia board’s decision to reinstate Huang “doesn’t excuse” him from testifying before Congress.

Ricketts is pushing for Congress to pass the Match Act, a bill that would pressure US allies to restrict sales and maintenance of advanced chipmaking equipment destined for China. It would not directly restrict Nvidia’s chip sales.
Companies based in allied countries that make semiconductor-manufacturing tools would be affected, such as the Netherlands’ ASML and Tokyo Electron in Japan.
Supporters argue that under the legislation, China would have greater difficulty developing its own advanced AI chips that would compete with Nvidia in the long term.
The top Democrat on the House intelligence committee, Representative Jim Himes, said Huang is still expected to appear for a closed-door interview on December 1 with three House panels.

Hakeem Jeffries, the incoming speaker of the US House of Representatives, said on Monday that Congress should include “ironclad” legislation to prevent AI technology from reaching China in the annual defense bill. That bill is a must-pass measure that funds the military and typically ​attracts bipartisan support. A Senate version of the legislation already includes several measures to crack down on China’s access to advanced AI chips.
Nvidia did not immediately comment on the criticism from Congress.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York said the reinstatement showed it was critical to pass legislation to toughen restrictions on US chip exports to China.
Trump on CNBC said he had pressed the Nvidia board to reinstate Huang and that he did not think the board would have done so without his action.
Republican Senator John Curtis, a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said he wanted answers about why the board opted to reappoint Huang as CEO.
“Last week, the board said it didn’t intend to reinstate him,” he said. “I’d like to know what changed.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: King Charles and Elton John pay tribute to Australian music legend Molly Meldrum
articles.summary: The promoter and broadcaster helped define the music tastes of Australians for decades.

blocks.text: King Charles and Elton John have paid tribute to Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum, who died aged 83 after a long illness.
Meldrum's family said he "passed away peacefully" at a hospital in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning.
The music promoter and broadcaster, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, helped define the nation's music tastes for decades, championing local artists like INXS and Kylie Minogue and global acts like Abba.
Known for his chaotic demeanour and trademark Stetson hat, he interviewed an array of stars, with the king on Monday calling him "a true giant of the music industry".

Born in Victoria in 1943, Meldrum displayed a love of music from an early age and went on to host the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's music television programme Countdown, and later a segment on variety show Hey Hey, It's Saturday.
Meldrum in 2014 became the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) Hall of Fame.
Meldrum lived with an acquired brain injury after falling from a ladder in 2011.
"Affectionately dubbed 'the Guru', Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music," a statement from Meldrum's family said.
Among his most famous interviews was a 1977 sit-down with King Charles, in which Meldrum could not calm his jitters.
He stumbled over his lines, declaring: "Your Royal Highness... Oh, oh, I'm sweating like a pig".

King Charles reflected on the infamous interview for Countdown's 40th anniversary special, saying: "There is an old showbusiness saying which warns never to work with animals or children. But nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum".
On Monday, an aide to the King said he had been "deeply saddened" to hear of Meldrum's death.

"His Majesty's interview with Molly is a moment he and many others will never forget - he hopes that interview will once again raise a few smiles as Australians honour Molly's legacy as a true giant of the music industry."
Elton John - a friend and regular interviewee - paid tribute to him as "an Australian legend and an institution", while pop star Kylie Minogue said she would be turning up the music in his honour.
"As a kid, I watched Molly Meldrum on Countdown every single weekend, in awe of the show and the magic it brought to our little TV in the lounge room."
"He championed so many Aussie artists and welcomed international artists to Australia in his own wonderful and inimitable way. I'm so grateful for his unwavering love and support."

Australia's Arts Minister Tony Burke said the country had lost an icon: "One of his greatest legacies will be the generations of Australians who grew up with his unmistakable enthusiasm and love of music."

articles.title: Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police
articles.summary: South African communities tell the BBC of measures they're taking to keep women safe after a wave of horrific killings.
articles.byline: Nomsa Maseko, Thuthuka Zondi, Eleanor Smallwood

blocks.text: Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police

blocks.caption: Image caption, Okuhle's body was found dumped near a river in August. She had two children, aged three and nine, and was a civil engineering student

blocks.text: Image source, Family handout
Okuhle's body was found dumped near a river in August. She had two children, aged three and nine, and was a civil engineering student
ByNomsa MasekoThuthuka Zondi and Eleanor Smallwood BBC World ServiceReporting fromEkurhuleni
Tuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook.
It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time.

Then one Saturday, two of Tuku's neighbours called him to say that they had seen that Okuhle had been reported missing by police on Facebook. They had also seen a photo of what appeared to be Okuhle injured.
"When I looked at this photo, I saw that the person in it was dead, and when I looked closer I realised it was Okuhle," says Tuku, 50.

After seeing the image, Tuku phoned a police officer he knew. The policeman confirmed the woman in the picture had been killed and her body dumped near a river in Kokstad, an agricultural hub in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, in the east of the country.
But because the morgue was closed for the weekend, it wasn't until Monday morning that Tuku was able to identify Okuhle's body.
When he did, Tuku saw she had been mutilated and her face badly beaten.
"It was very painful, so much that I cannot accept it."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Okuhle's father, Tuku, says he feels "ignored and unseen" by the government after his daughter's death

blocks.text: Image source, Thuthuka Zondi/BBC
Okuhle's father, Tuku, says he feels "ignored and unseen" by the government after his daughter's death
Okuhle had two children, aged nine and three, and was a civil engineering student.
She is among 581 women who were killed in the country between July and September, according to the South African Police Service.
Overall, there were 5,590 murders - 204 fewer than in the same period last year.
It is the first time police have broken down murders by gender, so it is unclear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease on previous years.

There has been a renewed national outcry this year about the scale of violence against women after the partially naked and bruised bodies of 12 women were found dumped in public areas in Ekurhuleni, a district to the east of Johannesburg, this summer.
South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and femicide - the intentional killing of a woman or girl - in the world.
Am I Next? Fear and Survival in South Africa
The BBC World Service visits communities struggling to confront widespread violence against women

In response to this summer's killings, President Cyril Ramaphosa promised safety audits across every municipality to identify and address dangerous spaces for women, as well as an increased police presence in the worst-affected areas.
But in places like Kokstad and Kempton Park, both in Ekurhuleni, the BBC World Service saw people taking the protection of women into their own hands.
For Tuku, that means investigating his daughter's killing himself.
Months after she was killed, he says no-one has been arrested.
"It was just silent after we buried Okuhle - there was nothing at all. I so wish the police would stand up and investigate."

He believes police failed to review CCTV footage from a local government building in the town that may have shown who his daughter was with on the day she disappeared. The footage is wiped every seven days, he says.
The BBC approached the South African Police Service for comment but at the time of publication, no response had been received.

The police service has previously acknowledged shortcomings in its overall response to gender-based violence and femicide, adding that it was continuing to invest in addressing these challenges. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has said there needs to be "greater efforts" to prevent violence against women and children.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The killing of women this summer sparked widespread protests across South Africa

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
The killing of women this summer sparked widespread protests across South Africa
According to a 2024 report by the South African Medical Research Council, the number of unsolved cases of femicide was growing.
This year, Amnesty International said South Africa's police service was "under-resourced, poorly equipped, and insufficiently trained to respond effectively and sensitively to gender-based violence".
Tuku says he is now searching for CCTV footage and seeking out people who knew his daughter in the hope of finding leads.
Despite Ramaphosa's promises, he has little faith anything will change.
"I listened to Ramaphosa. The government acts only when something happened. We in Kokstad, we feel like we are ignored and unseen. The government does not care for us."

Asked earlier this month by the BBC what progress South Africa had made to keep women safe, Ramaphosa said the government would be allocating extra money in February's budget to deal with gender-based violence.

Speaking as he cast his vote in local elections, Ramaphosa added that the government had increased police numbers in the last three years "and we will continue to do so, so that there can be more visible policing".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kokstad residents have started night-time patrols and are maintaining a curfew that advises children to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00

blocks.text: Kokstad residents have started night-time patrols and are maintaining a curfew that advises children to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00
Okuhle is not the only woman to be killed this year in Kokstad.
Between January and October this year, the bodies of five women and three very young children were found in the town, with arrests only taking place in two of the cases.
In response, this summer, the community set up street patrols and a curfew for women and children.
Since June, children have been told to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00.

Kamvalethu Cetywayo, 34, from a local neighbourhood watch group, leads a group of around 15 men who patrol crime hotspots in the town at night, including areas where bodies have been found or trouble has been reported to them.
The patrols tend to take place between Thursday and Sunday because this is when people drink alcohol most heavily, says Kamvalethu.
Most of the patrollers carry sticks, whips and torches, but Kamvalethu has a licensed gun. He says the group will call police when they need back-up.
Asked how he feels about restricting the freedoms of women and children, Kamvalethu says the curfew helps keep them safe, is voluntary, and a temporary measure until police arrest the killers.
"With the resolution we made with the community, we get to assist them with this, but if people are refusing there's nothing we can do."
Even so, not all victims are attacked at night or on the streets.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kgothatso says she was taking a taxi to work when the driver attempted to kidnap her

blocks.text: Kgothatso says she was taking a taxi to work when the driver attempted to kidnap her
Kgothatso Mojela was kidnapped on her way to work in 2018 in Kempton Park.
She was in a taxi when the driver locked the doors and started driving in the wrong direction.
When Kgothatso told him he had missed the turn, she says he started punching and slapping her.
"Immediately, I just knew my life was in danger," says Kgothatso, who is now 35.

Kgothatso says she forced the passenger door open and threw herself out of the moving taxi, badly injuring her knee and causing nerve damage to her eyes. Two security guards, who were nearby, came to her aid.
She says her attacker was later jailed for a number of crimes, including what he did to her, but was released last year. Kgothatso says she now fears for her life.
Yet while Kgothatso was attacked by a stranger, according to the South African Medical Research Council, 60% of women murdered in the country between 2020-21 were killed by an intimate partner.
In the wake of her attack, Kgothatso has made changes to how she lives, including buying an imitation gun to scare off would-be attackers.
She has also stopped running alone, and insists on someone accompanying her if she goes to meet a client she hasn't met before at work.
Such precautions are all too familiar to many women in South Africa.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Zama says her running group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles

blocks.text: Zama says her running group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles
In September police urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone, "particularly in isolated areas" - after the killing of 38-year-old mother Elizabeth Moselakgomo.
She vanished on 9 September while out running. Her badly bruised, partially clothed body was found dumped near a busy motorway in Kempton Park three days later.

It was a killing that resonated deeply within South Africa's running community, including sisters Zonke and Zama Mthethwa. They started The Pack, a women's running group in Johannesburg nine years ago. Elizabeth would sometimes attend The Pack events.
Runners across the city joined the search efforts following Elizabeth's disappearance, and took part in protests calling for violence against women to end.

Zonke and Zama's group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles. They also get cars to follow them and have started offering self-defence coaching to the women in their running group.
"We need to try and rally and create safe spaces for women to show up authentically and to do what they love doing," says Zama, 37.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at a prayer march to remember women who have been killed

blocks.text: Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at a prayer march to remember women who have been killed
Following her ordeal, Kgothatso moved from Kempton Park and now lives closer to her parents in another part of the country.
Her mother, a community activist, recently organised a prayer march to remember women who have been killed.
Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at the march.
Wiping away tears, she said: "To a survivor listening right now, I want to say you are not dirty, you are not broken beyond repair. You are not to blame and you are not alone."

blocks.caption: Graphic with Global Women written in white on a purple background, with blueish-purple arcs taken from concentrically arranged circles on the right.

items: This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

articles.title: Zack Polanski backs report endorsing Nato membership and maintaining nuclear weapons
articles.summary:
Position contrasts with Green party’s policies before 2024 election, as polls show just 17% of voters trust them on defence

Zack Polanski has given his backing to a paper that endorses…

blocks.text: Zack Polanski has given his backing to a paper that endorses Britain’s membership of Nato and the maintenance of the country’s nuclear weapons.

The Green party leader has welcomed a report from the Verdant thinktank that says the UK should remain in the military alliance and calls for the country to cooperate more closely with France on the maintenance of its nuclear weapons.

Party sources stress that its defence policies remain unchanged since 2024, when it went into the last election calling for the UK to sign the UN treaty on the prohibition of nuclear weapons and immediately begin dismantling its Trident submarines.
However, they added that Polanski’s endorsement of the report was part of a debate taking place within the party on how to reassure a broader group of voters on national security issues.

Polanski said: “At its core, national security is about food on the table, warm homes and safe communities. That makes it a progressive issue – and I welcome Verdant’s call for a comprehensive security framework that brings people from across the UK into keeping our country safe.”

Sacha Deshmukh, the author of the report, said: “Historically some progressives have shied away from recognising security threats. But the right has not been willing to accept the flaws in their policy solutions, so they are not always as strong as they should be – both sides need to change that.”

National security has often been seen as one of the Green party’s weak points with a YouGov poll last year showing just 17% of voters trusted the Greens on defence – the lowest of 18 different issues.

Concerns over the Greens’ positions on defence have driven some members to call for it to end its opposition to drones and anti-ballistic missiles, something that caused an internal rift ahead of its conference this year.
The Verdant report is likely to trigger another round of debate within the party, given that the thinktank, while independent, retains close links to the Greens.

The report calls for the government to rethink its national security strategy to focus more on value for money, such as by buying more weapons off the shelf rather than designing high-end bespoke systems for use by the British military.

It also calls for more investment in climate adaptation – something some in the green movement view sceptically as taking attention away from efforts to stop the climate deteriorating in the first place.
In two policy areas, however, Deshmukh calls for government policy to remain largely the same, despite previous calls from the Green party and Polanski personally for more radical change.
On Nato, he calls for the UK to remain a member but push for reform of its structures alongside allies within the alliance.
Such a position mirrors the official Green party policy, but contradicts what Polanski has previously said is his personal view.
He told the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast earlier this year: “Donald Trump has so much domination within Nato that I don’t believe it’s possible to reform Nato from within.”
And on the nuclear deterrent, Deshmukh argues the UK could not, and potentially should not, cancel the contract for the next generation of nuclear submarines, known as Dreadnought.

However, he adds that the country should seek to cooperate more closely with France on the missiles that will equip it, even though it is being developed to carry the US Trident missiles, which the UK currently uses.

Any form of commitment to the nuclear deterrent would be a sharp contrast to the promise the Greens made before the last election, when it said elected members would push for the UK to begin dismantling its nuclear weapons immediately.

articles.title: Robert Macfarlane says trust in Cop to deliver change on climate is ‘misplaced’
articles.summary:
Nature writer reveals in his first Reith lecture that he finds ‘much more hope’ in emerging alliances

We are “misplacing our trust” in the Cop climate summits and their “capacity to deliver…

blocks.text: We are “misplacing our trust” in the Cop climate summits and their “capacity to deliver consequential change”, according to Robert Macfarlane in this year’s Reith lectures.

In comments recorded before this week’s failure of the 31st UN climate summit to deliver an agreement on action to combat global heating, the bestselling author said he saw “much more hope” in emerging alliances such as the Santa Marta process, which is a smaller group of countries committed to phasing out fossil fuels as soon as possible.

“I would urge us to support these forms of collective reimagining away from ossified institutions that have failed to deliver,” said Macfarlane during the debate that followed his first Reith lecture, which will be broadcast on BBC Radio 4 on 24 November. Diplomats, scientists and activists including Al Gore have called for reform of the Cop’s requirement for a consensus after the failure of this year’s talks.

Inhis lecture, Macfarlane, a professor of literature and environmental humanities at the University of Cambridge whose books, including Underland and Is a River Alive?, explore global environmental crises, argues we must challenge the pervasive but wrong “human superiority complex” in western thinking which has supported centuries of planetary abuse, leading to the entwined climate and extinction crises.

The planetary crisis we are facing is a “crisis of the imagination as well as legislation”, said Macfarlane, because of a “default planetary operating system” that has arisen from Aristotle onwards and promotes the idea that humans are separate from the rest of nature, superior to it, and can thrive by conquering it.

The idea of human superiority spread by Christianity, the philosophers of the Enlightenment and Europeans who colonised other continents is so ubiquitous that it is barely seen by citizens or governments, and is embedded in everyday language, from “livestock” to “natural resources”.

“Governments speak easily of datacentres as critical national infrastructure but don’t seem to recognise that river systems and pollinator populations are also critical national infrastructure,” said Macfarlane.

He told the audience after the first of his four 2026 Reith lectures that the “end-times tech bro” was today’s “most charismatic and frightening contemporary expression” of the human superiority complex, and he criticised “planet B thinking” for promoting the idea of establishing a human colony on Mars.
“It is the ultimate act of consumption and disposal. ‘Hey bro, this planet’s done. Chuck it in the trash, let’s go and find another.’ Mars colonisation is the oligarch’s rapture dream,” he said.

Macfarlane is using his four lectures to reveal a burgeoning alternative way of thinking about our place on the planet which conceives of humans as not standing atop a hierarchical ladder but as nodes on a web of life that is connected to everything. Many Indigenous societies have practised such thinking for millennia but in the west it was first expressed, said Macfarlane, by the German polymath Alexander von Humboldt when he was exploring the Andes in 1802 and realised that “nature is a living whole” of which people were one small part.
after newsletter promotion

Despair at seemingly unstoppable global heating, oil wars and a chaotic technological arms race was “a luxury”, said Macfarlane, but he warned “hope” – “a verb with its sleeves rolled up” – involved real hard work.

“The first thing that anybody who is feeling helpless and hopeless should do is join a collective – find the folk who also love trees, who care about birds, who recognise that our life is absolutely inextricably tied to part of that larger living world,” he said. “Join your river guardianship group, drag the tyres out of the river on a Saturday morning. The best antidote to despair is repair. Start small; we build big.”

Macfarlane said young people, many of whom may succumb to the opposite of hope, which was not despair but “numbness”, must not be “terrified” by abstract threats but given opportunities to access nature and do hands-on work. He suggested partnering every British school with a farm and a tree-planting project “so that children are planting the trees that they then see grow throughout their lives”.

Asked about non-violent direct action by an audience member who had served a prison sentence for her role in Just Stop Oil protests that temporarily closed the M25 motorway, he said he would be willing to go to prison if he believed his peaceful direct action could have more impact than his writing, teaching and campaigning outside prison.

“What needs to change is not the nature of the protests that you and others have undertaken, which is peaceful protest, it’s the legislative environment that has sprung up around peaceful protest, particularly in the last three to five years,” he said, condemning the arrest and imprisonment of people in Britain for peaceful environmental protest.

articles.title: 'I'm not a hero,' says Arizona man who found lost toddler alone in the desert
articles.summary: Search parties with helicopters, K-9 units and heat-seeking drones scoured the rural dessert community of Eloy, Ariz. for hours looking two-year-old Vella Campillo after she wandered away from her…

image.caption: Body cam footage shows the moment police arrived on the scene after Arizona resident Jay Stewart found missing toddler Vella Campillo hiding in a bush in the desert earlier this month. (Pinal County Sheriff's Office)

blocks.text: As It Happens·New

Search parties with helicopters, K-9 units and heat-seeking drones scoured the rural dessert community of Eloy, Ariz. for hours looking two-year-old Vella Campillo after she wandered away from her backyard — all to no avail. Then Jay Stewart found her hiding in a bush.
Police, dogs and drones scoured area for 2-year-old to no avail. Then Jay Stewart found her in a bush
Jay Stewart has a lot of precious memories, but he says nothing compares to the moment he found two-year-old Vella Campillo alone in the cold, dark Arizona desert, wearing nothing but a diaper.

Police are hailing Stewart as a hero after he found the missing toddler who wandered away from her backyard last week, sparking a massive search-and-rescue operation in the rural community of Eloy, Ariz.
"I am so grateful to have experienced that life event, because there's no other feeling like it in the world," Stewart told As It Happens host Nil Köksal.
"That's No. 1 in my life, the most emotional moment I've ever had."
Vella was unharmed and has been safely reunited with her parents, police said.
LISTEN | Interview with Jay Stewart about finding Vella:
As It Happens6:16Arizona man describes the emotional moment he found a lost toddler alone in the desert
Vella was reported missing around 6 p.m., local time, on Nov. 17, according to the Pinal County Sheriff's Office.
Her parents, Joseph Campillo and Deanna Fritz, told Fox News affiliate KSAZ that she'd been playing in the backyard with her siblings under the care of another family member when she wandered off.
Officials from several police and fire departments spent hours scouring the area along with dozens of volunteers, two helicopters, K-9 units and heat-detecting drones, all to no avail.
Then, just after midnight, Stewart called Vella's name and saw her pop out of a tiny patch of plants in the desert.

"I spun around, and she jumped back down into this little bush … the size of, like, four dinner plates put together," he said. "She almost looked like she was swimming. Her little arms were moving around like she was treading water."
Pitch black and freezing cold
Stewart and his wife had been looking for Vella ever since the emergency alert hit their phones notifying people of a missing child in their area.
They spent two hours searching along the side of the road, he says, before heading home to check the news and bundle up in warmer clothes as the sun went down and the cold set in.
"The desert is kind of like being in a mine. It could be pitch black where you can't see anything. And that's what it was like," he said.
On their second try, they drove into the desert behind Vella's home on their ATV.
"I've lived out there 20 years and I fly over it all the time in our helicopter. So I know it like the back of my hand," he said. "It's my backyard."
Pinal County Sheriff Ross Teeple, right, awarded Stewart a plaque and a badge the day after he found a missing toddler near Eloy, Ariz. (Pinal County Sheriff’s Office)
Stewart says he'd separated from his wife as he wandered about a mile down a ditch calling Vella's name. He heard a yell, then saw her pop up and back down again.
He reached down, plucked her into his arms, unzipped his jacket and tucked her inside.
"She whimpered for about 15 seconds when I picked her up, and then once I snuggled her to me and got her, she seemed pretty happy," he said. "She warmed up pretty quick."
Stewart says she didn't make a peep until he dropped his phone while talking to a 911 dispatcher.
"And she went, 'Phone!' I started laughing. And I'm like, 'Yeah, baby, phone!' " he said. "It chokes me up. I can hear that little voice."

items: Indiana woman crashes car into ditch, survives on creek water for 6 days
This 77-year-old spent a night alone on a mountain. He raised over $30K for his rescuers

blocks.text: Within 10 minutes, he says, police and other searchers were on the scene.

Body cam footage released by the Pinal County Sheriff's Office shows Stewart holding the toddler on his hip. By that point, she was wrapped in a blanket provided by another searcher and chattering away happily in baby talk.
When the officer took Vella to check her over, the little girl clutched onto Stewart.
"She wouldn't let go of me," he said.
'The very best of our community'
At a news conference on Nov. 18, Sheriff Ross Teeple awarded Stewart a plaque and a badge for his community service.

"Your selflessness and willingness to get involved amplify the very best of our community," Teeple said. "Your actions remind us that every citizen has the power to make a meaningful difference and that sometimes, the greatest acts of service come from simply choosing to help."
But Stewart says he was just one of dozens of volunteers who showed up for Vella, and he happened to get lucky.
"I'm not a hero. I'm a searcher, just like everyone else was," he said.
He called the rescue the most emotional moment of his life, followed by the birth of his children and the day he married his wife.

"The reason I put it ahead of my kids is because I knew where my kids were. They weren't lost. I was holding them," he said. "But to find something that's lost like that, helpless and lost? I can only imagine what the parents were going through."
Interview with Jay Stewart produced by Chris Trowbridge

articles.title: Rights group details 'surge' in violent attacks on Palestinian health-care workers
articles.summary: Based on testimony from health-care workers, Physicians for Human Rights Israel says there’s been a 350 per cent increase in violence against Palestinian health workers by settlers and the Israeli…

image.caption: Palestinian men inspect torched vehicles following a rampage by Israeli settlers east of Ramallah, where Yousef Dihir works as a paramedic. (Mahmoud Illean/AP Photo)

blocks.text: World·New

Based on testimony from health-care workers, Physicians for Human Rights Israel says there’s been a 350 per cent increase in violence against Palestinian health workers by settlers and the Israeli military. Israel denies the report's claims.
Violence jumped 350% from 2022-2024, Physicians for Human Rights Israel says
For Yousef Dihir, a paramedic since 2008 in the West Bank, treating his fellow Palestinians has become a daily — sometimes lethal — risk.

Leaning against his ambulance in Ramallah, Palestine, earlier this month, he told CBC News about one of the many incidents of settler violence he's faced after receiving a distress call. On this particular occasion, three years ago, his son had come along as a volunteer paramedic.
"My son was injured, we were hit with glass in our faces when the gunshots broke out on the ambulance," he said. "They shot at the rear glass and the front glass."

In a report published this week, Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) says settler violence affecting health-care workers "surged 350 per cent" between 2022 and 2024 in the West Bank, from 93 violent encounters to 422.
Attacks on Palestinian medics in West Bank surge 350%: rights group

PHRI documented instances of violence against health-care workers through interviews with 25 paramedics, medics and emergency response workers, Dihir included, as well by accompanying paramedics and ambulance drivers during their shifts to see first-hand how they navigated checkpoints to get to patients.

PHRI says the uptick in violence has been particularly notable since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks that killed 1,200 people, saw 251 taken hostage and sparked a devastating war in Gaza that has left much of the territory in ruins and its two million people living in dire conditions.
Since then, PHRI says, "restrictions on medical care under the violent occupation have increasingly given way to direct attacks by Israeli forces and settlers on emergency medical services."
They say it's clear that the health-care workers were targeted in particular through "broader policies sustaining Israel's unlawful occupation of the West Bank."

items: Gaza is slowly moving beyond survival mode — 3 years after the war began
UN commission says Israel has continued to commit genocide in Gaza since truce

blocks.text: The number of obstacles blocking movement around the West Bank has also increased, from 642 in June 2023 to 925 in December 2025.
"Reaching patients, evacuating the wounded and transferring patients between medical facilities all depend on Israeli military approval," the report says.
"Interviewees describe physical assaults, threats at gunpoint, verbal abuse, humiliating searches and being prevented from reaching wounded or seriously ill patients."
The report notes an uptick in violent altercations between settlers and paramedics in the West Bank since Oct. 7, 2023. (Bashar Qaryuti/PHRI)

In 2025, the World Health Organization recorded a total of 233 attacks on health-care workers in the West Bank. And 38 attacks were recorded between January and April 2026, "35 of which involved obstruction of health care."
It is a violation of international law, said Milena Ansari, director of the Occupied West Bank at PHRI, at a news conference on Nov. 16.

Citing the Fourth Geneva Convention, which guarantees protection of civilians during armed conflict, Ansari said Israel has a responsibility to ensure medical services and public health access to "the occupied population."
"And this explicitly extends to Palestinian paramedics, ambulances and emergency medical teams."

items: Israeli settler violence at unprecedented levels during Palestinian olive harvest

blocks.text: IDF denies claims, condemns 'acts of violence'

The Israel Defence Forces (IDF) denied claims that their security forces were stopping medical teams from doing their work and "condemned all acts of violence against medical teams and ambulances," in a statement to CBC News.
"The IDF enables freedom of movement for medical teams through Judea and Samaria and coordinates the movement of Palestinian ambulances with relevant authorities in advance," the statement says.
Ansari said that's not enough.

items: Israeli settler violence at unprecedented levels during Palestinian olive harvest
Israeli strike on a Gaza hospital kills 6 people, including surgeon, health authorities say

blocks.text: "We should be setting a high standard of removing all checkpoints, removing all barriers that are between Palestinian communities and Palestinian territories," she said.

In one case, a paramedic described being kept away from an injured man. "I was standing close to the wounded man. I could have reached him easily, but the soldiers stopped me. He lay there bleeding until he died. Only then did they leave, and we were able to reach him," the paramedic recounted to PHRI.

The United Nations Office for Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said the highest number of violent attacks in the West Bank has been recorded in 2026 to date with over 2,000 attacks against Palestinians resulting in death or property damage.
Paramedics 'constantly on edge,' report says
PHRI is calling on Israel to end all violence against medical workers in the West Bank and ensure the unhindered passage of ambulances through checkpoints, gates and closed areas.
They are also calling on the government to investigate settler violence and prosecute all attacks against medical workers.
Multiple countries urge Israel to allow aid into Gaza
The PHRI report also documents the "severe psychological toll on emergency workers," with many noting feelings of distress, anxiety and sleep disturbances.
"All 25 described being constantly on edge, fearing they could be stopped, attacked or prevented from reaching patients," it says.
Dihir said one of his colleagues died in April 2023 during an altercation with settlers.
"He was shot in the head but he refused to stop," he said. "He was afraid for the lives of the injured." His patients survived the attack.
While Dihir admits he doesn't want to die, he says he's not scared.
"I don't care about religion, race, ethnicity or anything else. ... I only care that a person needs humanitarian help and I can do that."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Yasmine Hassan is a producer in CBC's Ottawa bureau. From there, she covers developments inside Gaza and the West Bank related to the Israel-Hamas war. If you have a story idea, send news tips in English or Arabic to yasmine.hassan@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte camp opposes 'sweeping' closed sessions for ICC prosecution witnesses
articles.summary: PRAGUE, Czech Republic - Former President Rodrigo Duterte"s defense team opposes the International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecution"s request for a “sweeping use” of closed court sessions for…

blocks.text: Published November 24, 2026 6:50am

PRAGUE, Czech Republic – Former President Rodrigo Duterte’s defense team opposes the International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecution’s request for a “sweeping use” of closed court sessions for witnesses, arguing it “unjustifiably infringes” upon his right to a public trial.

Duterte’s counsel Peter Haynes and his team state a “deep concern” over the scope of the Office of the Prosecutor’s (OTP) request for anonymity for most of its witnesses, and that the “same objectively justifiable risk” is not established in each witness category.

“The Prosecution is requesting that 55 out of the 69 of its witnesses testify anonymously, including 32 insiders. Further, it asks that 22 witnesses be authorised to give evidence entirely in closed session,” Haynes noted in a redacted filing released on November 23.
“Simply put, the Prosecution is requesting anonymity for 79% of its testifying witnesses, 40% of whom would then give evidence effectively in secret.”

Haynes argues that the high-profile status, increased media exposure, being government members or PNP officers, living in the Philippines or in the same area as Duterte’s supporters, or being known to the former president are “insufficient reasons, per se, to warrant protective measures.”

Duterte’s defense team asks Trial Chamber III to consider the “necessary and proportionate implementation” of using pseudonyms and face/voice distortions. It also raises “less stringent measures” such as the “targeted use of private sessions”.
“[T]hat would neutralise or mitigate the alleged risks to the same extent all the while respecting Mr Duterte’s rights,” Haynes noted.

Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang has requested special in-court security measures to “protect the witness’s (or another person’s) safety, physical and psychological well-being, dignity, and privacy”.

He argues these protections are warranted “in light of the high vulnerability of these witnesses,” or to “minimize the impact of testimony by providing psychological and emotional support to the witnesses.”

Although the Common Legal Representatives of the Victims (CLRV) back the prosecution’s request due to “prevailing political and social climate in the Philippines”, they suggest the court adopt a “comprehensive and prospective approach” in its assessment to prevent a “real risk of harm, intimidation and/or social ostracism” to witnesses and their families.
The defense’s opposition comes a few days before Duterte’s ICC trial opens, with limited public information on which prosecution witnesses Trial Chamber III will allow to appear in court.
Presiding judge Joanna Korner and fellow judges Keebong Paek and Nicolas Guillou have yet to publicly release their decision on protective measures for witnesses admitted in court. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
articles.summary: Megaspeed has been accused of funneling AI chips to China after a former executive's affair with Jensen Huang became public.

blocks.text: The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.
The US Department of Commerce announced on Monday that it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.

The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks, a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funneling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.
When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the Commerce announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month, when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had carried on an affair with Jensen Huang.
Alice Huang was thought by the US intelligence apparatus to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.
China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

Days later, another alleged affair surfaced involving Jensen Huang and the CEO resigned. On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he "convinced" the company and "made the deal".
The Commerce Department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years prior to the affair incident.

The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China. China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.
Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China, Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, is its largest customer.
