articles.title: Butt of the joke: Trump impersonator mocks president at Canada press dinner
articles.summary:
Carney watches on as comedian lampoons US leader and his interest in men’s backsides at correspondents’ event Ottawa

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, was joined on stage in Ottawa by a…

blocks.text: Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, was joined on stage in Ottawa by a Donald Trump impersonator who mocked the US president to raucous laughter from a crowd of politicians and journalists at a parliamentary press gallery dinner on Saturday.

With coiffed hair and an ill-fitting suit, comedian Mark Critch – who portrays the president on the sketch show This Hour Has 22 Minutes – danced on to the stage and lampooned the trade war Trump started as well as the president’s threats to annex Canada.
“We’re going to have a great deal,” Critch said, channeling Trump’s distinct mannerisms. “There’s only one thing standing in the way: me, because I’m crazy.”
The fake Trump continued that he was “so popular we just had a big, blue wave”, a reference to the Democratic rout of Republicans in this month’s US midterm elections.

He also mocked Trump’s frequent mentions of other men’s physiques, saying of the comedian Mark McKinney, who was portraying Carney, that he had “a great ass – doesn’t he? What a beautiful ass, he’s got such an incredible ass.”

He earned the most laughter of his short appearance for saying of Carney: “I don’t call him the governor to his face, because I’m a coward”. The real Trump has frequently attempted to insult Canada’s leaders by calling them governor, not prime minister, suggesting Canada is a US state.
The annual dinner, attended by media, political leaders and lobbyists, is often defined by carefully written jokes by the staff of party leaders.
Throughout his own 16-minute set, Carney poked fun at his political rivals, the media and the US president.
At one point, he remarked: “Damn, this is a tough room, and I’ve been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator.”
Clips of the dinner, including the crowd laughing at the president, have circulated widely on US media.
The newly appointed governor general, Louise Arbour, also gave a speech, including a nod to the prime minister’s decision to travel extensively around the globe.

“Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he’s supposed to be,” she said.
The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, also used the evening to poke fun at his own reputation.

“Some say that Mark has a controlling leadership style. There’s been reports that he yells and micromanages his staff. He acts like a miserable prick to journalists,” he said. “And when I hear things like that, I say once again, he’s stealing all my ideas.”

He attracted a stunned silence, however, for alluding to Justin Trudeau’s relationship with Katy Perry, saying, “Trudeau is running around the world doing to a faded pop princess what he did to Canada” while prime minister, a remark that was widely criticised as demeaning to the pop star.

The New Democratic party leader, Avi Lewis, who has not yet won a seat in parliament, took a shot at Carney’s early exit from the event, as well his own party’s dismal standings. “I do not have a seat in the House of Commons, but when I am given one at dinner, I stay there all night long,” he said.

articles.title: Canada adds Masar Badil group to terrorist entity list, citing status as alias for Samidoun
articles.summary: Canada's public safety minister announced Monday that Masar Badil had been added to the country's terrorist entity list, as an alias for Samidoun, a group which was added to the same list in 2024.

image.caption: Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree, seen speaking in the House of Commons last month, says the move to put Masar Badil on the terrorist entity list will provide law enforcement with additional tools to disrupt the group's financing and dismantle its networks. (Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Pres

blocks.text: World·New
Canada's public safety minister announced Monday that Masar Badil had been added to the country's terrorist entity list, as an alias for Samidoun, a group which was added to the same list in 2024.
Samidoun was added to list 2 years ago

In a news release, Public Safety Canada said "there is evidence" that Masar Badil — also known as the Palestinian Alternative Revolutionary Path Movement — and Samidoun "are the same entity" and "Masar Badil is acting as a faction/offshoot of Samidoun."

Public Safety Canada describes Masar Badil as an international movement "that claims to be working to build solidarity with Palestinian prisoners," but which operates under "the umbrella movement of Samidoun," which the government says the group has acknowledged having links to.
Samidoun and Masar Badil also have shared leadership and participate in joint events, according to the government.
Ottawa added Samidoun to the terrorist entity list two years ago, in a joint action with the U.S.
LISTEN | Samidoun listed as terrorist entity:
On The Coast8:50Vancouver-based Samidoun declared terrorist entity
The U.S., meanwhile, imposed sanctions on Masar Badil earlier this year. The state-side action saw officials also assert that the group is "inextricably linked" with Samidoun.

Several news outlets, including Global News and the National Post, reported Ottawa's move to list Masar Badil comes days before a conference organized by the group was scheduled to take place in Toronto.
The Public Safety Canada news release did not make mention of the pending conference.
Provides additional tools to law enforcement

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said in a statement Monday that the move to put Masar Badil on the list of terrorist entities, as an alias for Samidoun, will provide law enforcement with additional tools "to disrupt their financing, dismantle their networks, hold their members accountable, and to protect all people in Canada from terrorism and organized violence."
The Public Safety Canada news release said that a group that is put on the terrorist entity list then meets "the definition of a 'terrorist group' under Canada’s Criminal Code."

The Criminal Code, in turn, prohibits certain actions in relation to such groups, "including those related to terrorist financing, travel and recruitment," Public Safety Canada said in its news release.

The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs said in a published statement that it welcomed Ottawa's action on Masar Badil, but said the government had more work to do " to close gaps and enforce Canada’s anti-terrorism legislation."

articles.title: US adds Megaspeed, at center of Nvidia scandal, to a trade blacklist
articles.summary: The Trump administration has added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist after tensions over its failure to do so raised questions. The news came the same day that Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia's…

image.caption: The firm was suspected of helping Nvidia chips reach China despite US export restrictions [PHOTO: November 10, 2026]Image: Taryn Ng/AFP

blocks.text: The Trump administration added Megaspeed International, the firm at the heart of the Nvidia scandal, to a trade blacklist on Monday.
That means that the Singapore-based firm will not be able to obtain US technology, including semiconductors, without obtaining a license from the US government.
The news was reported by Semafor, an American news website.
US Commerce Department under scrutiny over Nvidia scandal: What to know
The US Commerce Department had been investigating whether Megaspeed was smuggling Nvidia chips into China for more than a year, according to the Financial Times.
But tensions at the Commerce Department broke into the spotlight after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with an executive at the Singapore-based firm earlier this month.

Politicians criticized Commerce Department Secretary Howard Lutnick for not having previously added Megaspeed to the department's so-called "Entity List" despite US intelligence warnings that the company was a possible front for smuggling sensitive AI chip technology to China.
Huang briefly lost his job over the scandal as US officials said the woman, Alice Huang, was a Chinese spy.

blocks.caption: Alice Huang attends a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang in Taipei in 2025 Image: TVBS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO on Monday, in a stunning reversal after his resignation just two weeks ago.

The New York Times reported last month that US authorities had concluded that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset who passed information to Beijing while developing a close relationship with Jensen Huang.
Beijing has denied those claims and called the spy accusations "groundless."
Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO
Nvidia shares soared more than 30% after the company announced it reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.
Some people were happy to see him back as president of Nvidia, as videos posted to social media show.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is on track to be the next speaker of the House, called the decision to reinstate Huang "indefensible, irresponsible, and incomprehensible" and vowed Congress would reinvestigate any wrongdoing by the company and the Commerce Department.

articles.title: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO after Trump intervenes
articles.summary: Share price surges as chipmaker reverses decision to remove chief executive after US president ‘convinced’ its board

blocks.text: Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive after Donald Trump directly intervened with the US AI chipmaker’s board of directors, in a stunning reversal of the tech billionaire’s downfall.

Speaking on Monday shortly after Nvidia’s surprise announcement that Huang had been restored to the top job – less than two weeks after he resigned – Trump said that he had “convinced” the board to do it. “I made the deal,” he told CNBC. Huang had resigned after reports of extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees.
“It’s very exciting news. I felt very strongly that he should come back,” the US president said.

Huang said he was “honored to return to Nvidia” and lead “one of the most consequential technology companies in the world”. He added: “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”

Nvidia shares surged on the news of Huang’s return, jumping 32% and adding more than $1tn (£760bn) to the company’s market value in New York on Monday, while Trump, who had persistently called for Huang’s return, said: “The country needs Jensen’s leadership.”

The chipmaker’s move to bring Huang back marks a sharp reversal from its board’s decision days earlier to rule out his return. The US vice-president, JD Vance, played a key role in discussions between the White House, Huang and Nvidia, according to the New York Times.

The US government has been investigating Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company formerly run by Huang’s alleged former lover, Alice Huang (no relation), over suspected diversion of semiconductors in breach of export controls, amid concerns Nvidia’s powerful AI chips may have been smuggled to China. Alice Huang has also been named in multiple reports as a Chinese spy.

The same day as Huang’s reinstatement, the US government announced it had added Megaspeed to a federal trade blacklist, preventing US companies from selling chips or other advanced technology to the Singaporean business.
Trump said on Monday the US government had no “evidence that [Jensen Huang] has engaged in any unlawful conduct” and that the attorney general, Todd Blanche, felt Huang was “exonerated”.

The US president told CNBC the US had to “protect our geniuses”, adding that the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, praised Huang at last week’s Apec summit in Shenzhen. Adding that he had talked to Nvidia’s directors, he said: “I’ve been speaking to the [Nvidia] board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it. I felt more strongly as I saw what was happening with the company.”

Nvidia’s share price had fallen by a quarter in the days after Huang resigned on 12 November. The falls were mirrored by a wider AI rout in global stock markets last week as investors feared new leadership at Nvidia could dampen prospects for AI companies that rely on the company’s chips to develop and operate AI tools such as chatbots, as well as having close financial ties with the chipmaker.

News of his shock reinstatement sparked a wider rally not just in Nvidia’s shares but on Wall Street as a whole, sending the Nasdaq composite index up 6.5% and the S&P 500 by 4.7%. The US dollar was lifted to a 19-month high.

In a statement, Nvidia said its board of directors had talked to Huang and were “satisfied with respect to Mr Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia”. Nvidia added that it had received input from “senior levels” of the US government and was confident his reinstatement “poses no national security risk”.

A senior Democrat, Elizabeth Warren, a senator for Massachusetts, said the decision was “reckless”, adding that it did not change the fact that Huang owed Congress answers about Nvidia’s compliance with trade restrictions on its powerful AI chips. He is due to give evidence to Congress on 1 December. The state of California is also investigating if Nvidia’s advanced chips ended up in China in violation of US restrictions.
She said his return increased the urgency of Congress passing export control bills “and making sure that Nvidia does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk”.
after newsletter promotion
Nvidia said an independent investigation into allegations Huang was the target of a Chinese intelligence operation was ongoing and “will proceed to conclusion”.

Harvey Jones, the Nvidia chair, who was appointed this month after Huang’s resignation, said: “The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.”

Huang built Nvidia from a video-game chip designer into the dominant supplier of AI processors, steering its roadmap, customer deals and Washington ties along the way. He resigned after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, whom US authorities suspect of spying for China, an allegation Beijing denies. It was also reported that Huang had an intimate relationship with two other Nvidia employees.

Trump praised Nvidia’s board for making “the correct and proper decision” and said: “The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at Nvidia in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy.”

It came hours after reports that Alice Huang had been in contact with an official in China’s spy agency while she was having an affair with the Nvidia boss. People with knowledge of US intelligence reports claimed she was in touch with the Chinese official until this autumn, according to the New York Times.

The Arm Holdings chief executive, Rene Haas, who had been approached to succeed Huang, has signed a new deal that will keep him in his current role until 2033. Huang had been replaced on a temporary basis by Colette Kress, Nvidia’s finance chief.

Elon Musk, who had called for Huang to return in an open letter backed by other Silicon Valley heavyweights, posted on X: “Welcome back the main man,” alongside a picture of him shaking hands with Huang. Trump said he had spoken to Musk “over the last week or so” about the Huang situation.
Sam North, a market analyst at the trading platform eToro, said: “Jensen Huang’s return underlines how much of the AI trade still rests on one man.”

Huang’s reinstatement has echoes of another recent real-life Silicon Valley drama. His return has taken place almost three years to the day since OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, brought back its chief executive, Sam Altman, after a similar bout of turmoil. Altman was removed by his board on 17 November 2023 but was restored five days later following an internal power battle.
In a post on X on Monday Altman wrote: “Jensen!”

articles.title: Court holds N.L. man over fear he will commit terrorist acts after threats against mosque
articles.summary: Facing eight charges and a court application used when there is a “fear of terrorism offence,” Matthew Collins was allegedly making threats against a mosque.

image.caption: Matthew Collins appeared by video in Gander provincial court Monday, Nov. 23. (Troy Turner/CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador
Facing eight charges and a court application used when there is a “fear of terrorism offence,” Matthew Collins was allegedly making threats against a mosque.
Collins accused of making bomb, remains in custody
Police say a Gander resident facing charges related to threats, hate and explosives is accused of making a threat against a mosque.

"The RCMP takes seriously any threats that undermine an individual’s sense of safety and security," the RCMP said in a statement on Monday. "Violent statements will not be tolerated, and we will continue to enforce the recently added Criminal Code provisions addressing hate-motivated offences."
The RCMP statement comes on the heels of the arrest of last week’s arrest of Matthew Collins.
Collins, also known as Maddie, remains in custody awaiting a bail hearing.
Collins is facing eight charges including ones related to possessing explosives, uttering threats and intimidation "regarding a religious property," the RCMP said.
There was also a court application filed that is used when there is a "fear of terrorism offence."

items: Gander resident Matthew Collins faces charges related to alleged bomb making

blocks.text: Collins appeared in Gander provincial court by video Monday after being transported to St. John’s for medical attention over the weekend.
The appointment was arranged Friday, when duty counsel cited fears Collins would self-harm.
The court heard today that, for "medical and safety" reasons, Collins was unable to travel back to Gander.

A social media account under Collins' name and likeness features several anti-Islamic posts, videos using knives as weapons, and images such as this one, showing a household drone attached to a small missile-shaped object. (Facebook)

The investigation into Collins began on Monday, Nov. 16, when the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary contacted the Gander RCMP for assistance in locating someone who was posting online content and alleged threats toward a mosque.
Collins’s apartment was searched and police seized electronic devices and other evidence relevant to the investigation.
"Police officers had reasonable grounds to fear that Collins may commit terrorism offences," Monday’s statement from the RCMP stated.
Terrorism expert Lorne Dawson says no judge wants to be the person who declines a terrorism peace bond. (CBC)
A ‘distinguishing’ feature in Canadian law, says professor
Lorne Dawson is a professor emeritus at the University of Waterloo specializing in terrorism.
He also co-founded the Canadian Network for Research on Terrorism, Security and Society.
He says the application before the court is similar to a peace bond and has been used in Canada many times by courts looking to restrict conditions placed on an accused.
"It's actually one of the distinguishing features in Canada, because a lot of the jurisdictions around the world don't happen to have a similar legal avenue on the books," Dawson said.
Dawson has done extensive research within communities dealing with radicalization.
He said these applications were common after the defeat of the Islamic state in Syria and Iraq in 2019.

"We had all kinds of individuals coming back to Canada or being brought back by the Canadian government," he said. "We're mainly talking about … Canadian women who married ISIS fighters or Islamic State fighters were in the camps and they had children, and they were brought back to Canada. Almost all of them were placed on peace bonds."
Gander resident remains in custody awaiting bail as terrorism risk is assessed

In recent years, he said the frequency of the bonds has declined, but they are still prevalent throughout the country. In many cases, Dawson said the bonds find their way to court following investigations into online activity of the perpetrators.

"I would think the most strong evidence presented is usually going to be people's online activity," he said. "It's pretty easy to gather this with the sophisticated abilities available for the Canadian security establishment."
Dawson says authorities must still document information relating to the investigation into why there is a fear of terrorism, and must document their suspicions.
In his experience, judges impose peace bonds to try to prevent future crimes.

"The fear of a terrorist attack is so strong, and the jeopardy to the public is so great — and there are so many unknown variables that may precipitate a terrorist attack — that they revert to these bonds," he said.
"No judge wants to be the person that declined the peace bond, and then the individual goes ahead and perpetrates a terrorist offence."
Matthew Collins appears in Gander provincial court on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026. (Troy Turner/CBC)
The peace bond application won’t be heard until after a decision on bail.
Collins’ next appearance is Wednesday in Gander provincial court.
Charges against Collins include:

items: Possessing explosive with intent to endanger life or damage property.
Possessing explosive substance.
Possession of prohibited weapon.
Uttering threats to cause death or bodily harm.
Uttering threats to damage or destroy property.
Intimidation.
Intimidation by using or threatening violence.
Included offence motivated by hatred.

articles.title: Jimmy Gomez to resign after House ethics panel finds evidence of sexual misconduct
articles.summary:
Democrat, who lost re-election bid, found to have made ‘unwelcome sexual advances’ towards House staffer

Jimmy Gomez will resign from Congress after a House ethics report released on Monday…

blocks.text: Jimmy Gomez will resign from Congress after a House ethics report released on Monday found “substantial evidence” that the California Democrat had “engaged in sexual misconduct”, including by “making unwelcome sexual advances and sexual contact toward a House staffer”.

The 19-page report from the House ethics committee found that Gomez “made unwanted sexual advances” toward a House staffer on two occasions, “including an incident in which he made sexual contact with her and another in which he was ‘forceful’ with her in his congressional office”.
Gomez, who represents parts of Los Angeles, lost his re-election bid earlier this month to the democratic socialist Angela Gonzales-Torres and was set to leave Congress in January.
Following the publication of the report, Gomez announced he would resign on 1 December.

The congressman said that he had “strong disagreements with the committee’s report and its conclusions” but said he took full responsibility for the “personal mistakes I committed outside of my marriage”.
Gomez said he cooperated with the investigation and responded voluntarily to requests for information.
The report stated that “Gomez’s conduct also reflects a broader environment of sexual misconduct and toxic working conditions in some Capitol Hill offices”.
The allegations against Gomez are the latest in a series of ethics investigations that have seen a slew of representatives resign from Congress or lose their bids for re-election this year.

In April, Eric Swalwell, also a Democratic representative from California, resigned from Congress following multiple allegations of sexual assault and misconduct that ended his bid for governor and saw a dramatic reshuffling in the race. Gomez was a co-chair of Swalwell’s gubernatorial campaign and stepped down after the allegations against Swalwell were made public.
That same month, Tony Gonzales, a Texas Republican, stepped down after admitting that he had an affair with an aide who later died by suicide.

In August, the Republican congressman Chuck Edwards, of North Carolina, announced he would not run for re-election after an ethics committee report determined that he “fostered a hostile work environment and engaged in sexual harassment” by giving gifts and lavishing attention on two young female staffers.

Cory Mills, a Florida Republican who is accused of a variety of ethical lapses, was defeated in the Republican primary. In October 2025, a Florida judge granted a protective order against Mills at the request of his former girlfriend.

In November’s midterm elections, Max Miller, a Republican from Ohio, lost his bid for re-election amid a House ethics investigation into drug use and domestic abuse allegations surrounding his divorce to Emily Moreno, the daughter Bernie Moreno, a Republican US senator.
The House ethics report on Gomez did not make any specific recommendations.
It noted: “The constitution charges the House with policing the behavior of its own members, and the House should take whatever action it deems appropriate in light of the committee’s findings.”

articles.title: Gisèle Pelicot 'humiliated' after nude photos sent to media to promote book
articles.summary: The publisher of an essay on coercive control apologises for "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".

blocks.text: Gisèle Pelicot has said she has been "once again humiliated" after nude images of her were sent to the media to promote a book about coercive control.
The 73-year-old told French broadcaster BFM TV she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay.

Pelicot made headlines across the world when she waived her right to anonymity in the trial of her then-husband Dominique, who was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious.
The publisher apologised, saying it would no longer print or promote the work after "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".
Pelicot told BFM: "I am deeply shocked that images from the most intimate part of my private life are being displayed and exploited for commercial purposes."
"Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt, as if the ordeal of the trial had not been enough," she said.
The essay was written by Sabine Prokhoris, a philosopher and psychoanalyst, who has previously criticised the Me Too movement.
French media reported that Tinbad, a small Paris publishing house, emailed nude photos of Pelicot taken by her ex-husband to some media outlets in order to promote the essay.
In a statement on its website, Tinbad said that no further print runs of the book would be produced beyond the 280 copies already in circulation.
"We offer our sincerest apologies to Ms Gisèle Pelicot," it said. The company also apologised to the author.
Tinbad said "no images of rape or pornographic videos" were sent to the media.
French news agency AFP quoted the blurb of the book as saying coercive control was "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy".
"These psychological situations, fundamentally ambiguous in nature, involve each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way," it said.
Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM the book "calls into question her status as a victim".
Prokhoris told AFP that she placed "full responsibility" for the "inappropriate" promotional campaign on her publisher.
Fifty men were convicted alongside Pelicot's ex-husband in 2024, in a case that made her a global feminist icon.

After her husband was arrested for secretly filming underneath women's skirts in a supermarket, she discovered she had been repeatedly raped by dozens of men, including her husband, while unconscious, over a period of nearly a decade.
Pelicot said she decided to waive her right to anonymity to show how "shame has to change sides" from victims to perpetrators.
If you have been affected by the issues in this story help and support can be found at BBC Action Line.

articles.title: Girl, 14, planned random killing of child at her former Winnipeg elementary school: Crown
articles.summary: A teen girl accused of planning to kill a child at her former Winnipeg elementary school was radicalized online and had a romantic fantasy about an American school shooter, a court heard before the…

image.caption: A Winnipeg teen who allegedly plotted to kill a kindergarten-aged child at random was granted bail by a judge Thursday. (Martin Diotte/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New

A teen girl accused of planning to kill a child at her former Winnipeg elementary school was radicalized online and had a romantic fantasy about an American school shooter, a court heard before the teen was granted bail last week.
Teen radicalized online by 'nihilistic, violent extremism culture,' expert testifies
WARNING: This story contains references to extreme violence involving children, and teen suicide.

A 14-year-old girl accused of planning to kill a child at her former Winnipeg elementary school was radicalized online and had a romantic fantasy about an American school shooter, a court heard before the teen was granted bail last week.

The girl, who cannot be identified under the Youth Criminal Justice Act, was granted bail by provincial court Judge Lindy Choy in a Winnipeg courtroom Thursday, according to recordings reviewed by CBC News. The teen is charged with one count of uttering threats.

She was admitted to a psychiatric unit for children and youth twice since July, with the most recent instance coming after her parents found written plans to kill a kindergarten-aged child at her former elementary school in early September, Crown prosecutor Jennifer Comack said.
The girl later expressed disbelief at her release from that facility, writing she had "fool[ed] everybody," Comack said.
"I have no idea how I got away with this with no legal consequences," the girl wrote in a journal seized by police on Oct. 15, according to the prosecutor.
"I told them it was just a joke and a hypothetical and they just ... believed it??? I mean, good for me."

Comack said the girl first gained police attention in July, when she was 13, after she tried to board a flight from Winnipeg to Toronto using credit card information she secretly obtained from her parents.

She planned to take a bus to Niagara Falls and walk across the Canada-U.S. border, where an 18-year-old man would have picked her up, Comack said. The girl later told her parents she was heading there to "participate in a suicide pact," Comack said.

items: Parents warned extremist groups are targeting a growing number of kids online across Prairies

blocks.text: The teen was initially admitted to the psychiatric unit after the July incident, but there was a "deep escalation" and "key shift" in her behaviour upon her release, as she began to engage with "nihilistic, violent extremism culture," Comack said.

Const. Andrea Lefort, a terrorism and extremism specialist with the Winnipeg Police Service, testified on Nov. 16 that the girl was radicalized online and is a "classic" example of young people who engage with "some of the most horrific" online content involving extreme violence and gore.

Lefort said the girl engaged with online communities that seek to emulate and "almost" fantasize about previous school attackers and mass killers, particularly Dylan Klebold — one of two teen gunmen who massacred 12 students and a teacher before killing themselves at Columbine High School in Colorado in 1999.
"We do see that with this online community, where in some cases, they will not just emulate them and want to mimic them, hence them planning their attacks," the constable said.

"But, in some cases, we will see a fantasy romance. And we do see that as well with [her], where we see her talking about her love for Dylan, and even talking about maybe seeing him at some point in the future, even though he's long since deceased."
The case represents "uncharted waters" for the Winnipeg Police Service, Lefort said.
'We are scared,' mother tells judge

The girl wrote about going to her former elementary school under the guise of visiting old teachers, hiding in the washroom and killing any child who entered, then "parad[ing] the corpse around the school to terrorize the children, before fleeing and killing herself," Comack said.
"What's the fun in killing yourself if you don't take anyone down with you?" the girl wrote, according to Comack.
She also wrote about the challenge in deciding what weapon to use, the prosecutor said.

"If I was in the [United] States, this would be an easy choice — a gun, duh — but I'm in Canada, which makes this a lot harder," she wrote. "I could use a hammer since the target would be a small child, maybe a knife. I think I'll bring both."

items: An extremist group has been linked to a Winnipeg terrorism-related case. What is M.K.Y.?

blocks.text: In another entry, the girl said she set the attack for Nov. 2, calling it "doom hour."
"Yay!!! It's nice having an official date."

Police and the former school were alerted about the planned attack in early October, court heard. The girl was arrested as she was discharged from the psychiatric facility on Oct. 15, which is when she gave a statement to police.
The girl told police she'd had unrestricted Internet access since age seven, and watched "cartel Mexican death videos as early as that age," Comack said.
"It is chilling to watch her, in her police statement, talk so matter of fact about killing a child," the prosecutor said.

As Lefort spoke about some extreme online communities' glorification of mass killers and their lack of empathy for the victims, someone on a court recording is heard saying, "So, just for the record, she is smiling right now."
The judge later asked the teen why she was smiling.
"It's awkward," the girl replied. "It's not smiling about the case or situation, it's more so just awkward."
The girl said she wanted to "get better," as she'd recently experienced "some really insane episodes," she said.

items: Violent extremism targeting kids online an 'escalating threat': Winnipeg police

blocks.text: "Sometimes, I just get really angry about something ... stupid."
The girl's mother, who was in the courtroom alongside her father, said they love and support their daughter but, "we are scared."
Comack said the Crown didn't oppose the girl's release but wanted to ensure she'll have no access to the Internet unless supervised by someone pre-approved.

The girl agreed to that condition, as well as staying away from her former elementary school, which CBC News is not naming to protect the girl's identity as required by the Youth Criminal Justice Act.
If you or someone you know is struggling, here’s where to look for help:

Kids Help Phone: 1-800-668-6868. Text 686868. Live chat counselling on the website.

articles.title: ICC sets procedure for external submissions in Rodrigo Duterte drug war probe
articles.summary: PRAGUE, Czech Republic - The International Criminal Court"s (ICC) Pre-Trial Chamber (PTC) I is setting out a standard procedure to process submissions from external entities regarding the court"s…

blocks.text: Published November 24, 2026 5:13am

PRAGUE, Czech Republic – The International Criminal Court’s (ICC) Pre-Trial Chamber (PTC) I is setting out a standard procedure to process submissions from external entities regarding the court’s investigation into the drug war linked to former President Rodrigo Duterte.

In an order released on November 23, PTC I instructed the ICC Registry to modify a template to be used by external persons or organizations seeking authorization to submit observations before the Chamber.

The template, which “reflects the situation name and number and the Chamber’s composition”, is adopted to ensure the “efficient and effective processing” of external submissions and “facilitate future interactions” from outside entities, the order stated.

Presiding judge Iulia Antoanella Motoc and her fellow judges, Reine Adélaïde Sophie Alapini-Gansou and María del Socorro Flores Liera, noted that requests for authorization must be limited to three pages.
“The Chamber clarifies that the template only applies to instances where a person or entity is requesting authorisation to make submissions.”

“The Registry will only transmit requests that abide by the instructions in the template. The Registry’s transmission filings, as well as the accompanying request and any other annexes, if applicable, shall initially be classified as confidential, unless cogent reasons require a more restrictive classification,” the order read.

PTC I cited the procedure for requests implemented in other situations, including an instance in the pre-trial phase of former President Rodrigo Duterte’s case when the Registry invoked Rule 103 of the ICC Rules of Procedure in April 2025.

That rule concerns inviting or granting permission from a state, an organization, or a person to submit written or oral observations on any issue the chamber finds appropriate or desirable “for the proper determination of the case”. The prosecutor and defense can respond to such amicus curiae observations.

In that April 2025 filing, the Registry asked authorization from PTC I to transmit the amicus curiae observation of a Hong Kong-based non-profit charity on the then-issue about the ICC’s jurisdiction to investigate drug war killings following the Philippines’ withdrawal from the Rome Statute.
Both the Office of the Prosecutor and Duterte’s then-counsel Nicholas Kaufman noted the filing as premature, with Kaufman stating were to raise a jurisdictional challenge "in due course".
The Chamber rejected the Registry’s request, but instructed it to inform external entities to use a template from Court Management Services to apply for authorization to submit observations.
In the present order, PTC I also cited similar implementations in the ICC’s investigation into Venezuela and Palestine.

In the Venezuela situation, the same pre-trial chamber rejected an applicant’s submission for lack of legal standing. In the Palestine situation, in which 64 states, organizations, and individuals were allowed to submit observations, a different pre-trial chamber reclassified more than 80 documents “in the interest of transparency and publicity of the proceedings”.

The Philippine situation concerns the crimes against humanity of murder, allegedly committed in the country between November 1, 2011 and March 16, 2019, during the drug war linked to Duterte when he was Davao City mayor and Philippine president.

PTC I, which handles the Philippine situation and heard the Office of the Prosecutor’s case against Duterte, previously ruled that the ICC retains jurisdiction over the alleged crimes when the Philippines was a state party to the Rome Statute, despite the country’s withdrawal on March 17, 2019.
Duterte’s case has been transmitted to Trial Chamber III, which will open its trial of the former president on November 30. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: UK sanctions top Myanmar military leaders after Rohingya genocide ruling
articles.summary: The UK is joined by several other nations in recognising an ICJ ruling that Myanmar carried out genocide.

blocks.text: The senior military leaders facing sanctions are Myo Htut Hlaing, Myo Min Tun, Myat Thet Oo, Kyaw Soe and Kyaw Swar Oo.

Miliband added that Myanmar's President Min Aung Hlaing, who was sanctioned by the UK in 2021, is "directly responsible for many of the atrocities that have happened" as he was head of the military at the time of the genocide in 2017.
He said: "Myanmar must stop ongoing violations, investigate, prosecute and punish perpetrators, and prevent such an atrocity from ever happening again."

Miliband also called for an "immediate pause in hostilities to enable humanitarian aid to get through, a stop to air strikes on civilians, and the release of political prisoners, as well as dialogue towards an inclusive political settlement".
The foreign secretary confirmed that new legislation would be passed to stop the supply of aviation fuel to the country, which was known as Burma until 1989.
Last week, he expelled Myanmar's defence attaché after the ICJ ruled the country had committed genocide during the brutal military campaign in 2017.
He told MPs on Monday the UK would raise the issue at the UN Security Council this week, and there would be a dedicated meeting in a fortnight.
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.

The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention, external.

In its ruling last week, the court determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were murdered during the clearance operation in the western Rakhine state that borders Bangladesh and the Bay of Bengal. Myanmar denied the claims against it.
Reports said that entire villages were burnt down, and that women and girls were raped.
Miliband said more than 1.2 million refugees fled and were being supported by Bangladesh.
Myanmar's leader during the genocide, Aung San Suu Kyi, was deposed by the military in 2021.
MPs heard that air strikes and violence from the Arakan army were still happening.

articles.title: Iranian singer and four others receive lashes after performance without hijab
articles.summary:
Western governments and human rights groups have criticised flogging as torture and a violation of international law

An Iranian singer and four members of her production team ⁠have each…

blocks.text: An Iranian singer and four members of her production team ⁠have each received 74 lashes after being sentenced for “offending public decency by producing and ⁠publishing obscene and ⁠immoral ​content online”, an Iranian news website said on Monday.
Parastoo Ahmadi and the four ⁠others were also handed two-year bans on artistic and musical activities and travel, the Emtedad website ⁠quoted lawyer Mostafa Nili as saying.

The case followed the ​release of a ‌video on YouTube ‌in December 2024 showing Ahmadi performing without the mandatory hijab alongside ‌male musicians in Qom, south of the capital Tehran, Norway-based human rights group Hengaw said.

Western governments and human rights groups have criticised flogging as torture and a violation of international law. Iran rejects accusations over ‌its human rights record, saying western countries should focus on their own human rights ​problems.

Rules requiring women to wear the hijab were a flashpoint during protests in 2022 after the ⁠death in custody of Kurdish Iranian woman Mahsa Amini, ​who was ​arrested for allegedly violating ​the dress code.
The rules have increasingly been ​flouted on ‌the streets of Tehran ​and ​beyond, and enforcement of the rules has also become more selective.

articles.title: What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war
articles.summary: Ukraine's sinking of a Russian battleship at a port in Libya raises the stakes of the war a notch, writes Frank Gardner.

blocks.text: Anchored up in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.

The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi, co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?
The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.
Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes, has called it "a dangerous escalation".
It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.
Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.

Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.

The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.

And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.
It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".

Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.

articles.title: Metropolitan police seize 893kg of cocaine hidden in boxes of oranges
articles.summary:
London force also makes eight arrests in operation centred on New Spitalfields Market in the capital

A tonne of cocaine was found hidden in boxes of oranges as part of one of the biggest…

blocks.text: A tonne of cocaine was found hidden in boxes of oranges as part of one of the biggest drug seizures in the history of the Metropolitan police.

Suspected cocaine weighing 893kg has been seized and eight arrests made as part of the investigation that targeted an organised crime group alleged to have been smuggling class A drugs into the UK. A Met spokesperson said the investigation was continuing.
Officers made arrests at London’s New Spitalfields Market on Sunday evening, the force revealed.
A large quantity of suspected cocaine was found hidden in boxes of oranges and five men, aged 27, 33, 41, 43 and 58, were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to supply class A drugs.
Video footage shows officers rifling through the cardboard boxes full of oranges to find black packages, featuring a drawing of a four-leaf clover, buried underneath.
Pictures taken separately on Sunday evening show blocks of suspected class A drugs filling five empty cardboard boxes. Some blocks feature the number “1100” on their front.

blocks.caption: Part of the Met drug haul. Photograph: Metropolitan police

blocks.text: The fruit and vegetable market, which relocated to Leyton in 1991, is the UK’s largest wholesale market, covering an area of about 13 hectares (31 acres).
A sixth man, aged 44, was also arrested nearby with 100kg of suspected class A drugs, the force spokesperson added.
Separately, police searched a property in Cheshunt, Hertfordshire, and arrested a 48-year-old man on suspicion of the same offence. Officers seized an estimated £450,000 in cash.

A lorry was also stopped near Maidstone and taken to Dover to be searched, with officers seizing around 250kg of suspected cocaine. The driver, a 50-year-old man, was also arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to supply class A drugs.
All eight men arrested remain in custody.

Det Spt Lindsey Billany, who is leading the Met’s investigation, said: “The seizure of these drugs, which would have been worth millions of pounds, represents a significant loss to this criminal enterprise and is one of the largest drug seizures we’ve seen.

“This policing operation demonstrates our focus on bringing down the drug traffickers whose trade fuels violence on London’s streets – and should serve as a warning to organised crime groups importing class A drugs.”

articles.title: Denmark: Top court backs hardline immigration "ghetto law"
articles.summary: Denmark's Supreme Court has found that evictions of "non-Western" residents do not amount to discrimination. The government in Copenhagen argues its "ghetto law" encourages integration.

image.caption: At least 60% of social housing units must be let to 'Westerners' by 2030 according to Danish lawImage: Liselotte Sabroe/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP

blocks.text: Denmark's Supreme Court on Monday ruled in favor of a housing association that terminated 91 leases in order to prevent the label "hard ghetto" being applied to their housing complex. The decision align's with Copenhagen's hardline approach to immigration.

The court on Monday upheld Denmark's 2018 "ghetto law," which allows for the relocation of "non-Western" residents from minority-heavy neighborhoods in order to foster integration. The Danish court ruling diverges from a top EU court decision last year that found application of the law could amount to discrimination.

The Danish laws requires social housing estates to rebuild, renovate and adjust their social mix if these become minority heavy, stipulating that 60% of apartments be rented to "Westerners" at market value by 2030.
Denmark: Forcibly resettling 'ghettos'
Denmark's hardline immigration policies making it a role model in the EU

Denmark's pioneering role in spearheading tougher immigration rules has made it a model for some in the EU. Denmark was also one of five countries that last week announced its intent to set up an asylum seeker deportation hub in Rwanda.
Danish Housing Minister Jacob Mark welcomed Monday's decision, saying it "strengthens security, social cohesion and integration."
The court's decision upheld a 2022 lower court ruling against seven tenants who fought their evictions in Nojsomhed, Helsingor, just north of Copenhagen.

In Monday's ruling, the law was found to be non-discriminatory when it comes to the eviction of "immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries" as it is not broadly based on ethnicity. The EU ruling focused on this particular aspect, saying the law would be discriminatory if criteria were race based, while ultimately allowing national courts to have the last say in the matter.

"The Supreme Court notes that applying the criterion of the law involves dividing people into two groups [immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries, and all other persons]. Both groups include a very large majority of different ethnic origins, and there will simultaneously be persons with the same ethnic origin in both groups," read the Danish court's ruling.
What is the EU-Rwanda return hub scheme?
Who is a 'non-Western' resident?
Tenants' associations estimate that 11,000 people across Denmark will have to be relocated to comply with the law.

The housing association in question issued a written statement saying that it was aware that the evictions would impact those affected, adding that it undertook measures to insure that residents found new homes.

According to Statistics Denmark's definition, "non-Western" countries include every country other than the 27 member states of the European Union, as well as Andorra, Australia, Britain, Canada, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, New Zealand, Northern Ireland, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, the United States and the Vatican.
Europe's asylum system is 'broken': Denmark's Stoklund

articles.title: Defence Department tops up cadet program after outrage over cancelled activities
articles.summary: The Defence Department will top up the budget of the cadet and junior ranger programs to allow weekend training and other activities to continue into the new year, Defence Minister David McGuinty…

image.caption: Cadets march in the parade to the cenotaph as part of the Remembrance Day ceremony in Fredericton, on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. (Stephen MacGillivray/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·Breaking

The Defence Department will top up the budget of the cadet and junior ranger programs to allow weekend training and other activities to continue into the new year, Defence Minister David McGuinty said on Monday.
Extra funding will allow weekend training, other activities to continue
The Canadian military put a halt to most cadet training in various parts of the country because of ongoing budget restraint within the department.

The halt involved weekend training and participation in competitions and was supposed to last until the end of the fiscal year in March. Weekly parade nights, however, were slated to continue while the department reviewed program funding.

The decision drew outrage from ordinary Canadians and the Opposition Conservatives. A number of Liberal MPs have privately said they've received a flood of constituent complaints and questions about the Defence Department's spending priorities at a time when billions of extra dollars are being spent on the military.

items: More cadets, more money, less training: Military defends controversial suspension
Cadets being told to stand down as Canada adds billions to defence
Funding cuts leave northern cadets out in the cold

blocks.text: McGuinty said the cadet program is vital for young people and the government will provide extra funding.
"We've heard your concerns about changes to planned activities," McGuinty said on his way into the House of Commons.
"We can confirm that additional funding will be provided to ensure planned cadet and junior Canadian ranger activities can continue for the remainder of this fiscal year."
It's unclear what the size of the budget bailout will be.
Restoring cadet activities, McGuinty says Canada's defence funding is not 'limitless'

It is an important reversal because just last week, the second-in-command of Canada's military stood behind the decision to pause the training and other activities until March 31 and the new budget year.

Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee told a House of Commons committee that membership in the cadets program has jumped by roughly 20,000 in the last few years and funding for the program has also increased to $265 million annually.
"Unfortunately, a lot of the cadet funding is front-loaded. It happens during the summer months," Topshee said on Thursday.
"And so they spent a large part of that expanded budget on summer training. And we didn't factor in the sizable increase in the number of cadets participating in the program."
Military's 2nd-in-command says increase in cadets led to temporary cuts

He said, despite the growth in the budget, the cadet program had "run up against a hard cap on the amount of money that they've been given" and that it was important for the department to live within its means.
On Monday, McGuinty defended the cadet program's handling of its budget, saying new entrants can walk through the door and sign up at any time and that makes managing the finances a challenge.
"When we look back and we see what the growth has been, it's been considerable," McGuinty said.
He added that a review of precisely how big the cadet program budget needs to be is ongoing.

items: Former N.L. cadets call on Canada to restore weekend training activities
N.B. cadet volunteers, parents push back as military halts flights, competitions

blocks.text: The initial decision to rein in the cadet program budget was just one part of a series of internal belt-tightening measures at DND.

While the Liberal government has drastically ramped up defence spending and has largely exempted the department from its expenditure review program, it has also told DND to focus its billions of dollars in new investment on priority areas, including the purchase of new equipment.
At the same time, the department is still subject to reductions planned in a previous federal budget, passed by the Trudeau government.
Those reductions in operations and maintenance funding continue to roll out this year with DND expected to find $459 million in savings.
McGuinty said the controversy over the cadets and the government's decision to cut the program some budget slack is important.
"It sends the message that we are responsible with financial expenditures, that we're responsible with Canadian taxpayers' money, that we have to live within a budget," McGuinty said.
"You know, it's important for Canadians to understand there have been significant increases in funding on the defence and the Canadian Armed Forces front, but that's not a limitless amount of money."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.

articles.title: Jennifer Lopez says being Latina limited her early acting roles. Not everyone agrees
articles.summary: Jennifer Lopez said being Latina limited her early acting opportunities, prompting her to create roles for herself — a claim that drew online criticism because of her high profile and extensive…

image.caption: Jennifer Lopez, pictured in Los Angeles in May, is facing online backlash after saying in a recent podcast interview that she believes being Latina made it harder to land acting roles in Hollywood. (Monica Schipper/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Jennifer Lopez said being Latina limited her early acting opportunities, prompting her to create roles for herself — a claim that drew online criticism because of her high profile and extensive career.
Some users criticized actor's comments, pointing to her extensive career
Jennifer Lopez says she received fewer acting offers in Hollywood than many people assume — and believes being Latina played a role.
In a Nov. 20 interview with the New York Times’ Popcast podcast, Lopez, who is Puerto Rican, said, "Even from the beginning of my career, I got offered things, but I was only offered a few things.
"I had to kind of create things for myself."
She said she did not fit the mold of "a white actress," adding that although casting has become more diverse over the years, performers may still have to create opportunities of their own.

items: Jennifer Lopez and Shakira vow 'empowering' Super Bowl halftime show
Jennifer Lopez files for divorce from Ben Affleck

blocks.text: Her comments drew criticism on social media, with some users pointing to her high-profile career and extensive filmography as evidence that her account does not add up.

Adrianne Curry-Rhode, a former America’s Next Top Model contestant, called Lopez's comments "next-level delusion" and criticized her acting. Other users similarly questioned her acting ability, arguing that her performances — not her ethnicity — could explain why she was not offered certain roles.

In an email to CBC News, a representative for Lopez said the remarks should be understood as referring to the 1990s and early 2000s, and said that other Latino actors had described similar constraints, citing performers John Leguizamo, Michael Peña and Eva Longoria.

Indeed, other racialized actors have made similar claims about getting major roles. But Toronto-based pop culture critic Rachel Ho, who has followed Lopez’s career since the late 1990s, says that although she is a hard-working performer whose accomplishments are sometimes dismissed, Lopez's visibility and range of roles may make it difficult for audiences to understand the limits she describes.
"I do think she must have faced a great deal of discrimination that we have no idea about, and I do think she has worked very hard to get to where she’s at," Ho told CBC News.
"But on the other hand, I do think she needs to have a little bit more awareness of her privileges, even as an ethnic woman, in this Hollywood space."
A career spanning film and music

Lopez’s breakthrough role came with Selena (1997), in which she portrayed Tejano singer Selena Quintanilla. She went on to star in Steven Soderbergh’s Out of Sight (1998) with George Clooney, as well as in romantic comedies like The Wedding Planner (2001) with Matthew McConaughey and Maid in Manhattan (2002) with Ralph Fiennes.
She has also pursued a major music career, releasing On the 6 in 1999 and J.Lo in 2001.
In her breakthrough role, Jennifer Lopez plays the titular character Selena in the 1997 biopic about the Tejano singer. (Ricco Torres/AFP/Getty Images)

Ho said Lopez’s success was largely shaped by her ability to work across acting and music at a time when several Latino performers were gaining mainstream attention. She described the period as a "Latin explosion," naming Lopez alongside Marc Anthony, Ricky Martin and Enrique Iglesias.

She also noted that Lopez has played characters whose ethnicity was not central to the story, and said this can make casting a Latino performer feel less complicated to studios than casting actors whose cultural background is treated as integral to a role. Furthermore, she pointed to Lopez's appearance, saying she could be cast in roles not explicitly written as Latina.

items: Record-setting crowd attends star ceremony for late singer Selena

blocks.text: Other actors describe barriers

Actors of other ethnicities have also questioned whether success guarantees access to meaningful work. Mahershala Ali, a two-time Oscar winner, discussed the issue on the podcast 7PM in Brooklyn with Carmelo Anthony, where he said a Black actor winning an Oscar doesn't guarantee a steady supply of high-quality roles.
"There’s more good actors than there is good material," he said.
Actor Mahershala Ali poses for photographers at an event in Beverly Hills in 2025. (Frazer Harrison/Getty Images)

Actor Halle Berry also recently spoke about the issue of race and casting. Berry became the first Black woman to win the Oscar for best actress in 2002, for her role in Monster's Ball. In a recent interview with the Cut, Berry said she had expected a surge of scripts after her win, but recalled directors questioning what casting a Black woman would mean for a film’s story and whether such a movie would sell overseas.

Ho said Lopez’s comments can sound tone-deaf when viewed against her fame and the number of roles she has secured. She recalled Lopez’s prominence in the early 2000s and said she would not describe the actor as struggling in the ordinary sense. Still, she cautioned against dismissing the possibility that Lopez faced discrimination or had to work around limited choices.

"I think she’s a fascinating celebrity," Ho said. "I genuinely love her, but … at her point in her career, and maybe it’s because she is in a bubble and she doesn’t really see the wider world around her."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Christine Pagulayan is a Toronto-based producer and writer with CBC News, currently with the Entertainment unit. She has worked in various roles at CBC News Network and The National. She has also worked as a multiplatform reporter in Toronto, Winnipeg, Halifax and Moncton. You can reach her at christine.pagulayan@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Australian politics live: Penny Wong to defend US alliance; Coalition condemns Vanuatu deal
articles.summary: • Get our breaking news email, free app or

blocks.text: Key events

items: 8m agoPenny Wong to defend US alliance
9m agoWelcome

blocks.caption: Tess Ikonomou

blocks.text: Tess Ikonomou
Coalition objects to security agreement with Vanuatu
The Coalition has come out against a security agreement with Vanuatu because of objections to “binding conditions relating to the achievement of renewable energy and climate targets”.
In June, the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and his Vanuatu counterpart, Jotham Napat, signed the Nakamal agreement in Canberra that rules out the use of its territory for foreign military bases.
Under the $500mn deal, Vanuatu stated it would “not permit its territory to be used for any foreign military base or infrastructure”.
But in dissenting comments released last night, Coalition members of a parliamentary committee scrutinising treaties said they did not support ratifying the agreement in its current form.

double quotation markWe acknowledge the legitimate concerns Vanuatu and other Pacific Island nations have regarding climate change and its impacts on their communities, economies, and national security. However, Coalition members object to clauses … that limit the ability of future governments to change current climate and energy policy settings, by creating binding conditions relating to the achievement of renewable energy and climate targets.
The Albanese government has forged a number of agreements, including new alliances with Fiji and Papua New Guinea, to deny China a military foothold in the Pacific.
A government spokesperson said the Coalition was “putting culture wars ahead of regional security. It is remarkable that the Liberals and Nationals continue to disrespect Pacific priorities.”
Penny Wong to defend US alliance
Penny Wong says abandoning the US would “surrender a central source of Australian strategic weight” at the moment the nation needs every tool available during global turmoil.
In a major foreign policy speech on Tuesday, the foreign affairs minister will take aim at opponents of the US alliance who present a retreat from the mutual defence pact as a “road to autonomy”.

double quotation markSuch a policy would surrender a central source of Australian strategic weight at precisely the moment we need every opportunity for influence available to us. What they would do is give us fewer choices and leave us more vulnerable, reducing our capacity to contribute to a regional balance in which our sovereignty can be protected.

The Greens are opposed to the Aukus security pact, under which Australia is set to acquire nuclear-powered submarines, in addition to the presence of the joint Pine Gap base in the Northern Territory.
Wong will also elevate artificial intelligence as a foreign policy challenge, warning the emerging technology is reordering lives, economies and militaries in ways not yet foreseen.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Krishani Dhanji with the main action.

Rising prices are the top concern among Filipinos, according to the latest survey by OCTA Research, according to a report in "24 Oras."
Forty-two percent said that the government's priority should be controlling the prices of goods and services.

articles.title: Israel seeks to jail Palestinian student activist without trial after dorm arrest
articles.summary:
Mahdi Tounsi appeared with visible bruising after being interrogated by police on his association with Israeli-Palestinian organisations

Israeli professors, students and rights activists are…

blocks.text: Israeli professors, students and rights activists are calling for the immediate release of Mahdi Tounsi, a sociology student at Jerusalem’s Hebrew University who has been held without charge for more than two weeks after he was seized from his dorm room.

The detention comes amid a racist campaign of delegitimisation against Palestinian citizens of Israel, whose votes were critical to stripping Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition of its majority in elections last month.
Police took Tounsi, 26, a criminology and sociology student from East Jerusalem who is active in Jewish-Palestinian campaign groups, from his dorm room on 8 November.
When he appeared by video link at a court hearing on 19 November he had visible bruises on his face, did not have the glasses he needs to see properly, and his hair and beard had been shaved.

Tounsi told his lawyer that police beat him in the dorm, in the patrol car and at the police station, Israeli media reported. Interrogators questioned him about his activism with Israeli-Palestinian organisations Standing Together and Ir Amim.
Both groups called for his immediate release and warned against using security agencies to silence political activity and critical speech.

“[This] could happen to any student and any one of us, especially in a month when the government is persecuting Arab citizens, from [journalist] Abed Abu Shehadeh to the leaders of Arab political parties,” Standing Together said in a statement, calling on the university to intervene to ensure a fair judicial process.

Ir Amim described Tounsi as thoughtful, gentle and a valued partner “in movements bringing Palestinians and Israelis together”, in a statement that also warned of “serious concerns for his safety, wellbeing, and right to due process”.

blocks.caption: Demonstrators call for the release of Mahdi Tounsi outside the Jerusalem district court. Photograph: Jess Flom/JNA/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: After losing the election, Netanyahu and his allies weaponised false accusations of mass fraud – Israel’s election commission validated the results – in an attempt to hold on to power by delegitimising the votes of Palestinian citizens of Israel.
The prime minister has also been accused of politicising security institutions in his campaign against Palestinian-led parties, and fostering a rise in racist rhetoric.

When police powers to hold Tounsi under the original arrest warrant expired last week, they submitted an order to hold him without trial in administrative detention, signed by the defence minister, Israel Katz.

The administrative detention law allows Israel to hold individuals for up to six months without charging them or allowing them to see evidence against them, although it has to be presented in a closed court.
Because the Shin Bet security force did not send a representative to the hearing on Tounsi’s detention last week, it was postponed until Tuesday.

Ahead of the court hearing, Jewish and Palestinian students demonstrated at universities across the country, including Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, with signs including “Free Mahdi” and “Kidnapping Palestinians will not silence justice”.
The university authorities did not inform his family, and his detention only came to light after concerned friends reported him missing.

Hebrew University said in a statement that it was notified about the arrest shortly before police seized Tounsi, that no university representatives were present when he was detained and police afterwards said the arrest took place “without unusual incidents”.
It did not directly address the allegations of police violence, his visible bruising, the shaving of his head and beard, removal of his glasses or the shifting legal framework.

“The university is not a party to the legal proceedings involving the student, and we do not have information that would allow us to comment on the circumstances leading to the arrest or on the ongoing legal proceedings,” the statement said.
“We are concerned for his wellbeing,” the statement added, saying the university hoped “that his rights will be fully respected throughout the process”.
Israeli police did not respond to requests for comment about Tounsi’s detention.

Tounsi is a resident of East Jerusalem, not a Palestinian citizen of Israel. Palestinians holding that status can move freely inside Israel and Jerusalem but are stateless and can not vote in Israeli national elections.

articles.title: Trump defers to appeals court over army plan to detonate bomb-making material in Iowa
articles.summary:
Environmentalists sued last week to stop detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide over health and pollution concerns

Donald Trump on Monday said he would defer to a federal appeals court on…

blocks.text: Donald Trump on Monday said he would defer to a federal appeals court on whether the administration moves ahead with plans to detonate several tons of degraded bomb-making material at an Iowa ammunition plant.
Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, where the plant is sited, and thousands more in surrounding areas could be affected by detonated material that could disperse in the air and land on the ground.

The detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide was initially planned for Friday, but the army has since changed the date three times after an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects.
They had most recently planned for a detonation on Wednesday, saying the weather was most favorable that day.

Environmentalists sued last week in an effort to stop the detonation, winning a stay from the appeals court pending a decision on the validity of an emergency permit approved by the US Environmental Protection Agency that cleared the way for the operation.
Trump said he preferred to take care of the volatile material as soon as possible and that a controlled detonation would be much safer.

“At the same time, have ordered the military not to do so until such time as the eighth circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming governor-elect Rob Sand agreeing to the operation,” Trump said in a statement.

If Sand and the court do not agree, Trump said the administration will have no choice but to not proceed with the planned detonation, adding that he would hold the incoming governor responsible for “any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation”.
